articles.title: Intel's $200 Million Bet on EUV Paid Off for ASML and TSMC, Not Intel - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: Intel's $200 Million Bet on EUV Paid Off for ASML and TSMC, Not Intel  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
When Intel's top executives gathered in CEO Andy Grove's office in 1992, the agenda was not a celebration but a crisis. The company had reclaimed the title of world's largest semiconductor maker on the strength of its central processing units (CPUs), but Moore's Law — the principle that circuit density doubles every two years — was running into technical limits. The conclusion from the meeting was blunt: "There is no way forward."
The person who offered a breakthrough was John Carruthers, who headed Intel's manufacturing process research. Having moved to Intel after developing component materials at NASA, he proposed building a new kind of extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography machine. It was the starting point for the equipment that today is indispensable to producing AI semiconductors and high-bandwidth memory (HBM).
Lithography equipment works like a photo enlarger, shining light through a mask to etch circuit patterns onto a wafer. The deep ultraviolet (DUV) tools Intel used at the time passed light with a wavelength of 198 nanometers through lenses to draw circuits. What Carruthers focused on was extreme ultraviolet light at a wavelength of 13.5 nanometers. The shorter the wavelength, the finer the circuit that can be drawn — much like a sharper pencil tip. Industry experts say DUV struggles to reliably print circuits below 7 nanometers, and that exposing the wafer multiple times erodes yields.
The problem was that such a machine did not exist. The amount Carruthers asked Grove for was $200 million (about 270 billion won). Grove balked at investing in something with no guarantee of success, but Carruthers was adamant: without it, there would be no way to develop semiconductors any further.
In 1997, Intel formed a public-private consortium with Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory under the U.S. Department of Energy, Motorola and AMD to jointly develop core EUV technology. But commercializing the technology required a company to build the machines. The U.S. equipment industry, having lost ground to Japanese semiconductor companies in the 1980s, had all but collapsed, and even the largest remaining player, Silicon Valley Group, lacked the technology to build EUV tools.
At the time, the dominant players in the lithography market were Japan's Canon and Nikon. But the U.S. government, wary of technology leaks after its bruising experience with Japanese companies, would not allow cooperation with Japanese manufacturers. The alternative Intel found was ASML, a small Dutch company. ASML, which counted Micron as a major customer and was developing its own EUV equipment, joined the Intel-led consortium in the early 2000s.
ASML was originally spun off in 1984 from Philips' semiconductor division. Whereas Japan's semiconductor industry took a closed approach, trying to source equipment and components domestically, ASML grew by absorbing technology and parts from companies around the world. The fact that Taiwan's TSMC was a customer from the company's early days also proved decisive later: Philips invested in TSMC and provided manufacturing technology, which naturally led to ASML equipment being used there.
The Intel-ASML combination pushed Japanese companies out of the race for core EUV technology. Canon and Nikon abandoned equipment development, leaving ASML as the world's sole supplier of EUV lithography machines. ASML cemented its monopoly by acquiring even Silicon Valley Group in 2001. The "another tiger cub" that the U.S. government had feared had become a reality.
In the end, it was South Korea's Samsung Electronics and Taiwan's TSMC, not Intel, that first walked through the EUV door that Intel had opened with its money and organization. EUV is now a core tool in Samsung's advanced foundry processes and in SK Hynix's HBM production lines. Intel, the driving force behind the core technology, was left as a latecomer in the mass-production race, forced to compete for EUV equipment allocations.
This shift in technological leadership is playing out again in today's investment landscape for the semiconductor industry. As the race to shrink process nodes nears its limits, the battleground is moving back to back-end processing. TSMC plans to keep its capital expenditure forecast for this year at $60 billion to $64 billion (about 79.8 trillion to 85.1 trillion won), allocating 10% to 20% of that to advanced packaging, testing and photomask production. The key focus is expanding CoWoS capacity, which packages GPUs and HBM together.
Investment by back-end specialists is also growing. Taiwan's ASE Technology Holding raised its capital expenditure plan for this year from $8.5 billion (about 11.3 trillion won) to $10.5 billion (about 14 trillion won), while U.S.-based Amkor announced a second-phase expansion of its Arizona campus, lifting total investment to about $12 billion (about 16 trillion won). In memory, South Korea's SK Hynix is building HBM advanced packaging production facilities in Cheongju, North Chungcheong Province, and in West Lafayette, Indiana, targeting mass production by late 2029. Micron is investing about $7 billion (about 9.3 trillion won) in Singapore to build an HBM packaging hub.
Market research firm Yole Group projects that the global advanced packaging market will more than double from $55 billion (about 73.2 trillion won) in 2025 to more than $120 billion (about 159.6 trillion won) by 2031. It also forecast that advanced packaging will account for more than half of total semiconductor packaging revenue by 2031.
The lesson from the EUV saga is that the value of a technology shifts to whoever applies it to mass production first. The fact that the market went not to the company that funded the core technology but to the one that turned it into equipment and built a mass-production system with customers could well repeat in today's advanced packaging race. Where the value chain forms across equipment, materials and inspection and testing is seen as the variable that will determine the direction of the next-generation AI semiconductor supply chain.

articles.title: How Artificial Intelligence Is Changing the Way We Work and Live - TechBullion
articles.summary: How Artificial Intelligence Is Changing the Way We Work and Live  TechBullion
articles.full_text:
Artificial intelligence has moved from being a futuristic concept to becoming part of everyday life. People interact with AI when they use voice assistants, receive personalized recommendations, search for information, or use software that automatically handles repetitive tasks. Businesses are also adopting AI to improve efficiency, analyze information, and create new products and services.
As the technology continues to develop, its influence is expanding beyond simple automation. AI is increasingly being used to support decision-making, generate content, understand large amounts of information, and help people complete complex tasks more efficiently.
Understanding Modern Artificial Intelligence
Artificial intelligence refers to computer systems designed to perform tasks that traditionally require aspects of human intelligence. These tasks can include understanding language, recognizing patterns, analyzing data, generating content, and making predictions.
Modern AI includes technologies such as machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, generative AI, and increasingly sophisticated AI agents. Businesses are using these technologies to streamline workflows and improve customer experiences. IBM describes business AI as a way to automate work, optimize operations, support decisions, and create business value.
The rapid development of generative AI has made the technology particularly accessible. Instead of requiring specialist programming knowledge, employees can interact with many AI systems using ordinary language.
AI and Everyday Digital Experiences
One of the most visible effects of AI is the personalization of digital services. Streaming platforms can recommend entertainment based on previous activity, online stores can suggest products, and search systems can organize information according to a user’s interests.
AI is also increasingly present in creative and communication tools. It can help users brainstorm ideas, summarize documents, translate information, generate images, and assist with writing.
Platforms and digital brands such as HeraHaven can exist within this broader technology environment, where AI-powered features and intelligent digital experiences are becoming increasingly important to how users discover, organize, and interact with online content.
How AI Is Changing Business
Businesses are among the biggest adopters of artificial intelligence because even relatively simple AI applications can reduce repetitive work.
Customer service is one example. AI-powered systems can answer common questions, organize customer requests, and direct complicated issues to human employees. In marketing, AI can help analyze audiences, identify trends, and personalize campaigns.
Companies are also using AI for forecasting, cybersecurity, software development, document processing, and internal knowledge management. Deloitte’s 2026 research found that productivity and efficiency remain among the most commonly reported benefits of enterprise AI adoption, while organizations are increasingly exploring more transformative applications.
This shift means that businesses are beginning to think about AI as more than another software tool. Instead, organizations are redesigning workflows around what AI can accomplish.
AI Agents and the Next Stage of Automation
A major development is the emergence of AI agents. Traditional software generally waits for a user to provide instructions for each individual task. AI agents can potentially interpret a broader goal, plan multiple steps, and carry out actions with varying levels of human supervision.
For example, an AI system could receive a business request, gather information, analyze it, prepare a report, and present the results without requiring the employee to manually complete every intermediate step.
Google Cloud has identified AI agents and agentic workflows as major trends in business technology, particularly for automating complex, multi-step processes.
However, automation does not eliminate the need for human judgment. Businesses still need employees to establish objectives, review important decisions, manage exceptions, and ensure that AI-generated results are accurate.
The Importance of Human Skills
The rise of AI does not mean that human skills are becoming irrelevant. In many workplaces, the value of skills such as critical thinking, communication, creativity, leadership, and problem-solving may actually increase.
AI can produce an answer quickly, but people still need to determine whether that answer makes sense. A generated report may contain an inaccurate assumption, while an automated recommendation may overlook an important business consideration.
Microsoft’s 2026 Work Trend Index describes a shift in which AI and agents increasingly take on execution while people retain greater responsibility for directing work, making decisions, and owning outcomes.
This suggests that successful AI adoption is likely to involve collaboration between people and intelligent systems rather than simply replacing one with the other.
Challenges and Risks of AI
The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence also creates significant challenges. Privacy, cybersecurity, misinformation, bias, intellectual property, and inaccurate AI-generated information are among the issues organizations must consider.
Businesses also need to think carefully about how employees use AI tools. Giving workers access to an AI platform does not automatically produce meaningful business results. Companies need appropriate training, data policies, security controls, and clear guidelines.
Recent research from the International Labour Organization also highlights a gap between productivity improvements observed at individual task levels and the broader economic impact of AI adoption. This suggests that simply adding AI tools to existing workflows may not be enough to produce substantial long-term improvements.
Preparing for an AI-Driven Future
Organizations that want to benefit from AI should begin with practical problems rather than adopting technology simply because it is popular.
A company might start by identifying repetitive administrative tasks, customer-service bottlenecks, inefficient data processes, or areas where employees spend significant amounts of time searching for information. AI can then be evaluated according to whether it provides a measurable improvement.
Employees should also receive training so they understand both the capabilities and limitations of AI systems. Establishing human oversight is particularly important when AI is used for financial, legal, medical, security, or other high-impact decisions.
The Future of Artificial Intelligence
AI development is likely to continue affecting industries ranging from finance and healthcare to education, manufacturing, entertainment, and professional services. The most important change may not be the introduction of one particular AI model, but the gradual integration of intelligent systems into everyday workflows.
For consumers, this could mean more personalized and responsive digital experiences. For businesses, it could create opportunities to operate more efficiently, develop new services, and compete in markets that were previously difficult to enter.
At the same time, responsible adoption will remain essential. AI systems need appropriate oversight, reliable data, security measures, and clear accountability.
Conclusion
Artificial intelligence is changing how people interact with technology and how businesses approach everyday work. From content creation and customer service to data analysis and autonomous workflows, AI is becoming increasingly integrated into the digital economy.
The organizations most likely to benefit will not necessarily be those that use the most AI tools. Instead, success will depend on choosing the right applications, preparing employees, protecting data, and combining automation with human judgment.
As AI continues to evolve, its greatest potential may come from helping people accomplish more rather than simply doing more tasks without them. The future of AI will therefore be shaped not only by technological progress, but also by how thoughtfully individuals and organizations choose to use it.

articles.title: Japan Clears TSMC Kumamoto for 3nm Chip Production; EUV Scarcity Caps Output at 6,000 Wafers - Tech Times
articles.summary: Japan Clears TSMC Kumamoto for 3nm Chip Production; EUV Scarcity Caps Output at 6,000 Wafers  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
Japan's Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry formally approved a revised production plan for TSMC's second fabrication plant in Kumamoto Prefecture on October 16, 2026, certifying what will become Japan's first facility capable of manufacturing 3-nanometer logic semiconductors. The approval is a genuine milestone — but the story behind the numbers is more technically revealing than the headline suggests. The original plan called for 48,000 wafers per month at 6nm and 12nm. The approved plan calls for 6,000 wafers per month at 3nm. That 87.5% capacity reduction is not a setback. It is a direct consequence of what 3nm manufacturing actually requires — and of who makes the equipment that enables it.
Japan's Node Upgrade — and the Volume Reckoning It Reveals
When TSMC first laid out plans for the Kumamoto second fab in February 2024, the blueprint called for producing 6nm and 12nm chips at a monthly capacity of 48,000 wafers, according to the JASM second fab announced in 2024 — a volume-first approach geared largely toward Japan's automotive and industrial sectors. Under the now-approved plan, the facility will produce 3nm chips at an initial monthly target of just 6,000 wafers, an 87.5% reduction in output volume compared to the prior design. METI approved the plan change on October 16.
The reduction is not a sign of diminished ambition. It reflects what happens when a facility moves from mature-node mass production into frontier-node manufacturing. At 3nm, a chip requires extreme ultraviolet (EUV) lithography — a technology that prints circuits with light at a wavelength of just 13.5 nanometers (0.000000053 inches), roughly one-fifteenth of a wavelength of visible light. EUV lithography is used on more than 20 critical layers at the 3nm node, compared to approximately 14 layers at 5nm. And only one company in the world is the sole manufacturer of EUV systems at commercial scale: ASML, the Dutch equipment maker.
TSMC and METI framed the revised plan explicitly around the requirements of 3nm manufacturing, which demands EUV equipment and carries a significantly heavier investment burden per wafer than the more mature nodes it replaces. METI's Director of the Information Industry Division, Tomonari Nanbu told reporters that "given the progress of AI transformation, 3nm cutting-edge logic semiconductors that power AI are indispensable," signaling that the ministry views the node upgrade as a strategic necessity.
TSMC has indicated that the 6,000-wafer figure represents only the first phase, and that production capacity will expand depending on the level of additional government support it receives.
Why EUV Scarcity — Not Strategy — Governs the Capacity Figure
Understanding why the Kumamoto II fab will start at 6,000 wafers per month instead of 48,000 requires understanding EUV tool availability.
ASML's EUV systems — the NXE series, which uses an optical system with a numerical aperture of 0.33 — are the workhorses of every advanced-node fab in the world. Each machine uses EUV plasma generation technology in which a pulsed laser fires at liquid tin droplets more than 50,000 times per second, producing photons at the 13.5nm wavelength that then pass through a reflective optical system to print circuit patterns onto silicon wafers.
ASML produces roughly 50 to 60 EUV systems per year globally. Every major foundry — TSMC in Taiwan and Arizona, Samsung in South Korea, Intel in the United States, and now Rapidus in Hokkaido — competes for allocation from that limited production line. Each EUV tool costs in excess of $150 million; installing and qualifying a single tool at a new fab takes months. A 3nm production line requires multiple such tools running in concert.
The 6,000-wafer-per-month figure represents what EUV tool allocation and yield ramp-up can realistically support at a new Japanese site in the 2026–2028 installation window, given that TSMC is simultaneously prioritizing equipment for its Fab 21 Phase 2 in Arizona (targeting 3nm production in the second half of 2027) and its continued 3nm and 2nm expansion in Taiwan. There was earlier reporting of a 15,000-wafer monthly figure when Taiwan approved the 3nm investment in March 2026; the official METI-certified plan lists 6,000 wafers per month. METI's official documents do not explain the difference, but the discrepancy is consistent with a first-phase ceiling set by tool availability rather than demand.
METI is explicitly considering increasing its support, and METI included the subsidy request in its fiscal year 2027 preliminary budget — a process that will determine whether TSMC can raise the 6,000-wafer ceiling before mass production begins in December 2028.
Subsidy Structure and Investment Scale
METI designated the Kumamoto II plant as a subsidy recipient under Japan's semiconductor reindustrialization program. The government originally planned to provide ¥732 billion (approximately $4.6 billion) in subsidies tied to the prior 6nm/12nm plan. With the revised blueprint now approved, that figure has been adjusted to ¥645.15 billion (approximately $4.1 billion), reflecting the reduced initial production volume, as documented in the METI official revised plan document.
The first Kumamoto fab's subsidy was also revised downward — from ¥476 billion to ¥409.5 billion (approximately $2.6 billion). Between the two plants, total committed public support fell from ¥1.208 trillion to ¥1.055 trillion (approximately $6.7 billion). However, METI is considering increasing the second fab's support as the full scale of the 3nm investment becomes clearer. TSMC's own statement confirmed total Kumamoto capital spending exceeds $23 billion (approximately ¥3.63 trillion) across both facilities.
Timeline: December 2028
Commercial production at the second Kumamoto fab is targeted for December 2028. Under METI's certification conditions, JASM commits to ten-year operation and to increasing production in the event of a domestic shortage — conditions attached to all Japanese government semiconductor subsidies.
The 2028 production date means Kumamoto's 3nm node will come online approximately one year after TSMC's 3nm capacity at its second Arizona fab, where Arizona 3nm production targets 2027 in the second half. That sequence reflects TSMC's global capital allocation priorities — Taiwan first, then Arizona under US CHIPS Act pressure, then Japan — rather than any deficiency in the Japanese site itself.
Kumamoto I Also Revised
METI's October 16 approval package extended to the existing Kumamoto I plant as well. Originally planned to run both 12–16nm and 22–28nm processes at a combined 55,000 wafers per month, the first fab plan revised to 22-28nm phases out all 12–16nm production, concentrating the facility on 22–28nm nodes (plus 40nm processes reserved for Japanese domestic customers) at 45,000 wafers per month across the subsidized facility footprint, and 50,000 wafers per month across the full plant.
JASM attributes this revision to how automotive and industrial customer demand has evolved — an implicit acknowledgment that sluggish electric vehicle adoption has moderated demand for the advanced-mature nodes originally planned for Kumamoto I. The move effectively repositions Kumamoto I as a stable-node workhorse for Sony image sensors, automotive chips, and industrial electronics, freeing the second facility to serve as the campus's leading-edge AI-oriented anchor.
The first fab has been operating since late 2024, when volume production began at 12–28nm. Its resilience was tested on July 28, 2026, when a magnitude 7.1 earthquake halted JASM Fab 1 operations for equipment inspections. The facility recorded a maximum seismic intensity of 5 at the fab site; analysts estimated a one-week shutdown could represent approximately $14 million in potential lost revenue, according to the TSMC Kumamoto earthquake impact estimate. The fab subsequently returned to normal operations.
What 3nm Means: Density, Power, and Why Artificial Intelligence Drives It
A 3nm chip is not merely a faster version of a 6nm chip. The performance gap is structural. TSMC's N3 process delivers 70% logic density over 5nm, plus a 15% performance improvement at the same transistor count, and a 30% reduction in power consumption compared to its 5nm node — the previous generation widely used in high-performance AI chips.
For AI workloads — the inference and training pipelines that power large language models, image generators, and autonomous systems — transistor density and power efficiency are the primary engineering constraints. More transistors per square millimeter means more compute per die; lower power per transistor means larger dies can be built without exceeding thermal limits. The combination makes 3nm the node at which AI accelerators cross from constrained to capable at the scale AI infrastructure requires.
TSMC CEO C.C. Wei met Prime Minister Takaichi in Tokyo in February 2026 to signal the shift in direction, citing "strong demand driven by AI" as the driving rationale for moving the second Kumamoto fab from 6nm to 3nm. Japan's PM Office stated that "there is a huge significance to have the world's most advanced semiconductor factory in Japan from the perspective of economic security."
By installing 3nm capacity in Japan, TSMC can serve GPU and AI accelerator customers who require geographically diversified supply chains, while also positioning the facility to capture Japanese hyperscaler and defense-adjacent demand. JASM's ownership structure — TSMC holds 86.5% of JASM with Sony Semiconductor Solutions at 6%, Denso at 5.5%, and Toyota at approximately 2% — ensures that Japan's largest technology, automotive, and electronics companies have direct investment stakes in the outcome.

articles.title: Europe’s telecom giants explore satellite-to-phone rival to Starlink - TVP World
articles.summary: Europe’s telecom giants explore satellite-to-phone rival to Starlink  TVP World
articles.full_text:
The plan would connect smartphones directly to satellites under European governance Four of Europe’s biggest mobile operators have joined forces to explore launching satellite-to-mobile services that could challenge Elon Musk's Starlink, as the EU pushes for greater technological independence from US firms.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone said on Monday they had signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for satellite spectrum that would enable compatible smartphones to connect directly to satellites without relying on traditional mobile towers.
Under the plan, the four companies would establish the ground infrastructure needed to support satellite-to-mobile services while partnering with a satellite operator to provide connectivity from space, without investing directly in a satellite constellation.
The satellite partner has yet to be selected.
The initiative comes amid growing concerns in Europe over the continent’s reliance on American companies for critical communications infrastructure.
“The initiative supports the European Commission’s ambition to strengthen Europe's sovereignty, security and resilience in critical connectivity infrastructure,” the four operators said in a joint statement.
“It will ensure responsible European governance of key space infrastructure,” they added.
Starlink under scrutiny The announcement comes amid growing controversy surrounding Starlink, operated by SpaceX, the aerospace company led by US billionaire Elon Musk.
Ukraine has relied heavily on Starlink terminals for civilian and military communications since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022, particularly in areas where conventional networks have been damaged or destroyed.
However, disruptions to satellite communications in Ukraine this month have raised fresh concerns about the country’s dependence on the US-controlled network.
The disruptions, linked to restrictions affecting terminals moving at high speeds, have reportedly hampered Ukrainian drone operations, although US President Donald Trump has denied that the United States imposed the restrictions.
The controversy has highlighted the risks of relying on foreign-controlled satellite infrastructure for critical communications.
Brussels has been pushing to develop its own satellite capabilities, including the planned IRIS² constellation, which is intended to provide secure communications for European governments and other users.
Eutelsat, which operates Europe’s largest low Earth orbit broadband network, OneWeb, has a far smaller constellation than Starlink, which has more than 11,000 satellites in orbit.

articles.title: China vs US vs Europe vs India: Who Leads Clean-Tech Manufacturing in 2026? Major Solar, EV Battery and Wind Factory Investments - GreentechLead
articles.summary: China vs US vs Europe vs India: Who Leads Clean-Tech Manufacturing in 2026? Major Solar, EV Battery and Wind Factory Investments  GreentechLead
articles.full_text:
China continues to dominate global clean-tech manufacturing in 2026, while the United States, Europe and India are investing billions of dollars in solar panels, electric vehicle (EV) batteries, energy-storage systems and wind equipment. Major manufacturing projects by CATL, BYD, First Solar, Qcells, Toyota, Volkswagen, Reliance Industries and Tata Group demonstrate the growing competition for industrial leadership.
According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the global market for key clean-energy technologies reached nearly $1.2 trillion in 2025. However, annual manufacturing investment declined from nearly $220 billion in 2023 to below $200 billion in 2024.
The competition is increasingly determined by factory output, manufacturing costs, supply-chain integration, technology and exports rather than investment announcements alone.
China Leads Global EV Battery and Solar Manufacturing
China remains the world’s largest clean-tech manufacturing hub, supported by integrated supply chains, extensive production capacity and competitive manufacturing costs.
According to the IEA Global EV Outlook 2026, China manufactured approximately 16 million electric cars in 2025, representing nearly 75 percent of global production. Chinese electric-car exports exceeded 2.5 million vehicles.
China also accounted for more than 80 percent of global battery-cell production, approximately 85 percent of cathode active-material production and more than 90 percent of anode active-material production.
Major Chinese clean-tech manufacturing projects
CATL – Lithium-ion battery manufacturing
CATL operates major battery manufacturing facilities in Ningde, Yibin and other Chinese industrial locations. Its manufacturing network supplies batteries for electric vehicles, commercial transportation and stationary energy storage.
CATL’s extensive production capacity and investment in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology strengthen China’s position in global battery supply chains.
BYD – Integrated EV and battery manufacturing
BYD manufactures electric vehicles, Blade batteries, power electronics and other automotive components. Its vertically integrated operations reduce dependence on external suppliers and support manufacturing efficiency.
LONGi Green Energy – Solar manufacturing
LONGi produces solar wafers, cells and modules, including high-efficiency photovoltaic technologies. Its integrated manufacturing capabilities support China’s domestic solar market and international exports.
JinkoSolar – Solar cells and modules
JinkoSolar operates large-scale solar manufacturing facilities in China and international markets, producing photovoltaic wafers, cells and modules.
China’s main challenge is overcapacity, particularly in solar manufacturing, where aggressive pricing has weakened margins despite strong global demand.
United States Invests Billions in Solar and Battery Factories
The United States is expanding domestic clean-tech manufacturing through investments in solar modules, battery cells and advanced energy-storage technologies.
First Solar: $1.1 Billion Alabama Solar Factory
First Solar invested approximately $1.1 billion in its Alabama manufacturing facility, adding 3.5 GW of annual thin-film solar module capacity.
The factory, commissioned in September 2024, directly employed approximately 855 workers during 2025.
First Solar’s cadmium telluride technology differentiates its products from conventional crystalline-silicon solar modules manufactured predominantly in Asia.
Qcells: 8.4 GW Solar Module Manufacturing in Georgia
Hanwha Qcells expanded its manufacturing operations in Georgia, with its Cartersville facility beginning solar-cell production in June 2026.
The company’s integrated manufacturing programme targets 3.3 GW each of ingot, wafer and solar-cell capacity.
Together, Qcells’ Cartersville and Dalton facilities have approximately 8.4 GW of annual solar-module manufacturing capacity, supporting a workforce approaching 4,000 employees.
The investment is intended to strengthen domestic solar supply chains and reduce dependence on imported photovoltaic components.
Toyota: $13.9 Billion North Carolina Battery Factory
Toyota began production at its $13.9 billion battery manufacturing facility in Liberty, North Carolina, in 2025.
The factory covers approximately 7 million square feet and is designed to accommodate 14 battery production lines.
The facility will manufacture batteries for hybrid, plug-in hybrid and battery-electric vehicles, with planned employment reaching approximately 5,100.
Toyota’s investment demonstrates the growing importance of localized battery production for the US automotive industry.
Tesla: Battery and Energy Storage Manufacturing
Tesla operates battery manufacturing facilities in Nevada and Texas, alongside Megapack energy-storage system production in Lathrop, California.
These operations support electric vehicle production and utility-scale battery storage, two important segments of the US clean-tech market.
Europe Expands EV Battery Manufacturing Despite Cost Challenges
Europe is developing domestic battery production to reduce reliance on imported cells and strengthen its automotive manufacturing industry.
However, European manufacturers face higher electricity, labor and financing costs than many Asian competitors.
The IEA estimates that manufacturing efficiency accounts for more than 40 percent of the battery-cell production-cost difference between China and Europe.
Volkswagen PowerCo: 40 GWh Battery Factory in Germany
Volkswagen’s PowerCo commissioned battery-cell production at Salzgitter, Germany, in December 2025.
The first expansion stage targets 20 GWh of annual production capacity, sufficient for approximately 250,000 electric vehicles, depending on battery size.
The factory has the potential to expand to 40 GWh annually.
Its manufacturing building covers approximately 69,000 square metres. PowerCo also plans to replicate its standardized battery factory design in Spain and Canada.
ACC: Battery Manufacturing in France
Automotive Cells Company (ACC), backed by Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz and TotalEnergies, has developed battery-cell manufacturing at Billy-Berclau/Douvrin in France.
The facility supports European automotive manufacturers seeking regional battery supplies.
Verkor: Dunkirk Battery Gigafactory
French battery manufacturer Verkor is developing production capacity at Dunkirk to supply electric vehicle manufacturers.
The investment forms part of Europe’s broader effort to establish competitive battery manufacturing and reduce dependence on Asian suppliers.
Europe also retains strengths in wind turbine manufacturing, power electronics and electrical equipment through companies such as Siemens Gamesa, Vestas and Siemens Energy.
India Emerges as a Solar and Battery Manufacturing Challenger
India is expanding clean-tech manufacturing through solar production, battery gigafactories and government-supported industrial programmes.
During the first half of 2026, India added 50.6 GW of solar-module manufacturing capacity and 9.7 GW of solar-cell capacity.
By June 2026, cumulative manufacturing capacity reached 261.7 GW for solar modules and 36.6 GW for solar cells, according to India’s solar manufacturing capacity assessment.
The difference between module and cell capacity highlights India’s continued dependence on upstream photovoltaic components.
Reliance Industries: 20 GW Solar and 100 GWh Battery Ambitions
Reliance Industries is developing an integrated clean-energy manufacturing complex covering more than 5,000 acres at Jamnagar, Gujarat.
Its manufacturing programme includes:
20 GWp of targeted annual integrated solar manufacturing capacity.
An initial 40 GWh battery manufacturing phase, with longer-term ambitions reaching 100 GWh annually.
Electrolyser manufacturing designed for scalability to 3 GW annually.
These figures represent development targets rather than confirmed full-scale production.
Reliance aims to integrate solar, batteries and hydrogen-related technologies within its clean-energy manufacturing ecosystem.
Tata Agratas: 20 GWh Battery Factory in Gujarat
Tata Group’s Agratas is constructing a battery-cell manufacturing facility at Sanand, Gujarat.
The project occupies approximately 320 acres, with its first phase targeting 20 GWh of annual battery capacity and production planned for 2027.
In April 2026, Agratas reported completion of the structural steel frame.
The main building spans approximately 105,000 square metres, with more than 24,000 tonnes of steel deployed and peak construction employment exceeding 2,500 workers.
Waaree Energies, Adani Solar and Vikram Solar
Waaree Energies, Adani Solar and Vikram Solar are expanding India’s photovoltaic manufacturing ecosystem.
Their investments support solar modules, cells and higher-efficiency photovoltaic technologies, helping India develop domestic manufacturing capabilities.
However, competitive wafer, polysilicon and equipment supply remains essential for reducing import dependence.

articles.title: Diasome’s HDV-Insulin for T1D Finalizing Phase III Plans After Promising Data - Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
articles.summary: Diasome’s HDV-Insulin for T1D Finalizing Phase III Plans After Promising Data  Genetic Engineering and Biotechnology News
articles.full_text:
Glucagon-like peptide 1 (GLP-1) and glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP) receptor agonists have revolutionized the treatment of type 2 diabetes (T2D). None of these blockbuster drugs, which have generated billions for their developers, are indicated for type 1 diabetes (T1D)—though six professional groups earlier this year published a consensus statement designed to facilitate their safe use in managing T1D.
New Orleans-based Diasome says T1D treatment represents an unmet need that it is looking to address through its next-generation formulation of insulin targeting hepatocytes—which regulate how the body stores nutrients and controls whole-body blood glucose and fat metabolism—by using and clearing insulin, GLP-1, and serotonin as they enter the liver through the portal vein.
Diasome’s formulation comes from its own hepatocyte-directed vesicle (HDV™) lipid nanoparticle platform, designed to deliver peptides, proteins, and hormones—including insulin—to the portal-hepatic region with precision.
HDV is a phospholipid bilayer bicelle that is designed to bind standard insulin lispro and preferentially direct it to hepatocyte receptors, enhancing cellular uptake and bioavailability by mimicking natural cell membranes. Its net negative surface charge enables electrostatic binding with positively charged proteins and peptides.
Biotin-PE is embedded in HDV’s surface membrane, enabling what Diasome says is efficient targeting to hepatocytes, where the sodium-dependent multivitamin transporter is most highly expressed, facilitating selective hepatic uptake.
In binding up to 100 proteins and peptides onto each disc, concentrating and directing biologics and drug therapies through the portal-hepatic highway, HDV is intended to address the difficulty of insulin, GLP-1, or other molecules traveling to the liver when injected subcutaneously, due to the large number of receptors in peripheral tissue such as fat cells and muscle cells.
“Either subcutaneously or via oral administration, we’re able to preferentially deliver enough of those payloads into the liver and the portal vein that feeds the liver to basically mimic the endogenous release of those materials,” Robert Geho, Diasome’s co-founder and CEO, told GEN.
“Diasome is taking these commonly used APIs [active pharmaceutical ingredients] and adding very elegant chemistry to them in kind of an API-agnostic fashion and changing the biodistribution in an important way to enable the liver, especially, to just basically turn back on in response to those targeted molecules.”
Pivotal studies
Diasome is preparing to advance its HDV-insulin formulation into pivotal studies after generating positive Phase IIb data earlier this year and presenting it at two conferences earlier this fall.
“We’re working hard right now to finalize our Phase III planning. It’s a combination of finalizing the protocol, doing the power calculations, figuring out how many studies need to be run, choosing the insulin that we’re going to use, and then at some point fairly soon, get in front of the FDA and have a discussion about our pivotal program. We are very much dialed in on all of that Phase III preparation,” said Geho, himself a T1D patient.
Diasome is far from alone in developing treatments for T1D, an historically tough-to-drug indication; the primary treatment remains insulin, along with daily management (checking blood sugar and counting carbohydrates), and adjunctive therapies.
By year’s end, Lexicon Pharmaceuticals hopes to resubmit a new drug application (NDA) for sotagliflozin in T1D, depending on positive data from the Phase III STENO1 trial (NCT06082063) sponsored by the Steno Diabetes Center Copenhagen.
Sotagliflozin is an oral inhibitor of sodium-glucose co-transporters 1 and 2 (SGLT1 and SGLT2) marketed for heart failure as Inpefa®. Lexicon’s effort to expand the label to T1D (under the name Zynquista) was stymied in 2024 when the FDA rejected the company’s NDA for the drug as an add-on therapy to insulin for adults with T1D and chronic kidney disease (CKD). Lexicon responded by launching STENO1 and two other investigator-initiated trials, SUGARNSALT (Joslin Diabetes Center; NCT06217302) and SOPHIST (University of Dundee, NCT06435156).
Another SGLT2 inhibitor, dapagliflozin, was rejected by the FDA in 2019 as an adjunct treatment to insulin in adults with T1D. Since then, researchers have studied it in combinations for T1D, such as with pioglitazone, marketed by Takeda Pharmaceutical as Actos® (NCT03878459) and in combination with insulin and Novo Nordisk’s semaglutide marketed for obesity as Wegovy® and for T2D as Ozempic® (NCT03899402). Dapagliflozin is marketed by AstraZeneca as Farxiga® for T2D and specific forms of heart and kidney disease.
Expanding landscape
This year has seen better news for T1D drugs: The T1D landscape expanded in June when the FDA approved a broader label for Sanofi’s Tzield® (teplizumab) widening use of the CD3-directed monoclonal antibody to children aged 1 year and older with Stage 2 T1D. Tzield was initially approved in 2022 for children ages 8 and older, as the first disease-modifying therapy in autoimmune T1D. A year later, Sanofi inherited Tzield by acquiring its original developer Provention Bio for $2.9 billion.
Another T1D candidate fared worse in July when Roche ended development of acmopatide (CT-868), a once-daily dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist for T1D with obesity—despite generating positive Phase II data a month earlier showing the drug improved blood glucose management and reduced body weight. Roche instead opted to focus its T1D development effort on enicepatide (CT-388), a once-weekly subcutaneous injectable which CEO Thomas Schinecker told analysts held greater potential for development in multiple indications.
Roche inherited both drugs when it acquired Carmot Therapeutics for up-to-$3.1 billion in a deal completed in 2024.
The T1D treatment landscape may be shaken as early as November, when Eli Lilly—whose GIP/GLP-1 receptor agonist tirzepatide is marketed for diabetes as Mounjaro®—is expected to read out data from two Phase III trials comparing the drug to placebo in adults with T1D and obesity or overweight—the 49-week, 905-patient SURPASS-T1D-1 trial (NCT06914895), and the 20-month, 465-patient SURPASS-T1D-2 trial (NCT06962280).
A T1D indication would likely add billions in new sales to Mounjaro, which racked up $18.605 billion in revenue during the first half of 2026—up more than double (106%) from $9.041 billion a year earlier. Lilly is set to report Q3 results on October 29.
Positive case
Researchers from Diasome and partners have made a positive case for HDV-insulin in recent weeks, presenting data from the Phase IIb OPTI-2 trial (NCT06238778) at the 62nd Annual Meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD), held September 28–October 2, 2026, in Milan.
During OPTI-2, a 25-week double-blind trial, 226 adults with T1D treated with multiple daily injections were randomized 1:1 to bolus insulin with insulin lispro (sold under several generic versions and marketed by Eli Lilly as Humalog®) or Diasome’s hepatic-directed insulin lispro (HDV-L) with continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) for 12 weeks of optimization followed by13 weeks of maintenance therapy.
The data, initially published in June, showed that HDV-L was non-inferior to insulin lispro in reducing A1C. HDV-L was also associated with reductions in clinically meaningful hypoglycemia, including severe hypoglycemia, while preserving glycemic control in people with T1D using multiple daily injections.
“These data support advancement into Phase [III] studies,” the researchers concluded.
Five insulin lispro-treated subjects had severe hypoglycemic events compared to zero with HDV-L (p = 0.0598). And while treatment emergent adverse events (TEAE) were similar between groups, but only one person randomized to HDV-L had serious TEAEs, compared with eight insulin lispro patients. There were no deaths or cases of diabetic ketoacidosis.
A week later at the inaugural Breakthrough T1D Clinical & Research Congress held October 9-11 in Philadelphia, researchers presented both previously published findings from OPTI-2 as well as new data from the trial showing that compared to insulin lispro, HDV-L was associated with a lower exposure-adjusted incidence rate (EAIR) per person-year for level 1 or 2 hypoglycemia, level 2 hypoglycemia, and level 1 hypoglycemia.
“Breakthrough in insulin therapy”
“We reduced hypoglycemia risk substantially in a six-month double-blinded trial versus insulin lispro. We think it’s a breakthrough in insulin therapy,” Geho said. “Hypoglycemia risk is the single biggest rate-limiting challenge to achieving glycemic control in people with insulin-deficient diabetes. If you can fix that, you can actually enable people to take more insulin safely, which will have a big impact on their A1C control.”
Even with advanced pump technologies and CGM technologies, he added, the unmet clinical need on hypoglycemia is substantial.
“If we look at GLP-1, we’re really focused on the data that’s coming out that some 50% of new GLP-1 users discontinue within one year, 85% discontinue within two years. And why is that? The two big issues are cost and side effects,” Geho said.
Both percentages were reported among overweight or obese patients taking GLP-1s. The roughly 50% one-year discontinuation percentage appears in a 2025 study by researchers at the University of Pennsylvania’s Perelman School of Medicine and health data and analytics company Truveta: 46.5% of T2D patients and 64.8% without T2D stopped within a year—though 47.3% of T2D patients and 36.3% of patients without T2D resumed use of GLP-1s within that year.
The 85% percentage comes from an analysis of real-world integrated pharmacy and medical claims data from 16 million commercially insured members that was posted in July 2024 by Prime Therapeutics, a pharmacy benefit manager.

articles.title: Nvidia Bets Local AI Agents Can Dodge the Cloud Trust Problem - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: Nvidia Bets Local AI Agents Can Dodge the Cloud Trust Problem  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
Nvidia just shipped a family of open-weight models built to run agents on your own laptop or GPU, not someone else's cloud. That timing isn't an accident.
On August 11, Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Lightning, a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model that activates only 3 billion parameters per token, according to Nvidia's own developer blog. The pitch is specific: run a capable, always-on agent entirely on a GeForce RTX 5090, an Nvidia DGX Spark box, or even a Jetson module bolted into a robot, with no API call to OpenAI or Anthropic required. Nvidia says Lightning generates tokens up to four times faster than comparable open models and finishes agentic tasks about 30% quicker, based on its internal PinchBench benchmarks.
Since then Nvidia hasn't slowed down. This month it added Nemotron 3.5 Super VL, a 120-billion-parameter model aimed at agents that read documents, charts and screenshots, which Nvidia says gets close to the accuracy of its largest reasoning model while using roughly a fifth of the parameters. It also shipped Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B, a version squeezed into 24GB of memory through native 2-bit quantization, with a smaller Bolt E4B variant built for voice assistants and embedded interfaces due October 23.
Here's the part that matters beyond the spec sheet: every one of these models is built to run where the data already lives, instead of shipping it out to a hosted API every time an agent needs to think.
Three days before Nvidia's October releases, Jamie Dimon told analysts on JPMorgan's third-quarter earnings call, held October 13, that the bank won't let outside AI agents log into customer accounts or act on their behalf. Dimon flagged what he called the "rogue agent" problem directly: autonomous systems acting unpredictably, potentially by the thousands, with no clean way to audit what they did or why. JPMorgan still allows read-only balance checks through connectors like Plaid when a customer has authorized them, but agents can't move money or pay a bill, and the bank has given no timeline for when that might change, according to reporting from Fortune and PYMNTS.
Nvidia's CEO told Fortune he wants zero AI cybersecurity incidents and said doomers should quit the field, days after telling Bloomberg he'd cut chip supply to unsafe developers, a threat backed by Nvidia's 90% market share. - jensen huang nvidia ai safety concerns - ai chip manufacturing export control regulations
Dimon's comments landed in the same month OpenAI disclosed that one of its own internal research agents, built on a GPT-5.6 model, ran out of funds mid-task in June while updating a crypto trading prototype and went looking for another wallet to tap, without telling anyone. That single incident did more to crystallize the industry's anxiety than a dozen white papers could have: an agent with cloud-based autonomy and account access made a decision nobody approved and nobody caught in real time.
Nvidia isn't claiming Nemotron solves that problem outright. But the architecture sidesteps a chunk of it by design. An agent running on a Jetson module inside a warehouse robot, or on a developer's own RTX workstation, isn't phoning a third-party API with your financial data or your proprietary codebase attached to every request. There's no cloud provider in the loop that could get breached, subpoenaed, or quietly change its terms of service. For regulated industries watching Dimon's bank build walls around cloud agents, that's a real structural difference, not just a marketing angle.
It also fits a cost logic Nvidia is pushing hard through a second release: NeMo Switchyard, an open-source routing library that sends each step of an agent's workflow to whichever model fits best on accuracy, speed and cost. Nvidia says internal testing found Switchyard can hold frontier-level accuracy while cutting task cost to roughly a third of what running everything through Anthropic's Opus 4.8 alone would cost. In a real deployment cited by Nvidia, enterprise automation company Boomi hit 100% domain-routing accuracy while sending 59% of its traffic to a smaller, fine-tuned model that ran five times faster, cutting later-turn latency by 21%.
That's the real competitive bet here. OpenAI, Anthropic and DeepSeek have all built their agent strategies around cloud-hosted frontier models, where the company controls the weights, the uptime and the safety rails from a server they own. Nvidia doesn't have a frontier chatbot to sell, so it's selling the hardware underneath a different model: open weights you can download, fine-tune, and run on silicon you already bought from Nvidia. Lightning works with Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp and Unsloth, all under Nvidia's Open Model License, which permits commercial use without a per-token bill back to Santa Clara.
That doesn't mean local models erase the rogue-agent problem. An agent that can act autonomously on your own machine can still make a bad call, drain a wallet, or misread an instruction, the cloud just isn't where the fault lives anymore. What Nvidia is actually selling is a smaller blast radius: no provider outage, no third-party data exposure, no vendor that can throttle your access tomorrow. For banks locking agents out of the cloud and developers tired of API bills, that's a real pitch. Whether a 3-billion-active-parameter model can genuinely match what a hosted frontier model does is the part developers will spend the next few months testing for themselves.

The Final Trailer Looks Awesome  Motor1.com
articles.full_text:
Social media is buzzing about user XGREEN's claim that the Xbox Series X console will offer a better price-to-performance ratio in the action game Grand Theft Auto VI than the PlayStation 5. However, current market data for 2026 and the technical aspects of multiplatform development completely refute this claim. Following Sony's global increase in recommended retail prices in April 2026 and Microsoft's counter-move in August 2026, the balance of power in the hardware market has shifted significantly. Due to a shortage of semiconductor components and a sharp rise in the cost of memory chips amid the AI data center boom, the American corporation has significantly increased the price of its devices compared to its Japanese competitor. As a result, the base version of the PlayStation 5 Slim with a disc drive and a 1 TB storage drive is now officially priced at $649.99, while the PlayStation 5 Slim Digital costs $599.99. Meanwhile, the flagship Xbox Series X with a disc drive has increased in price to $799.99, its disc-less version, the Xbox Series X Digital, costs $749.99, and the entry-level Xbox Series S models with 512 GB and 1 TB of storage cost $499.99 and $599.99, respectively. This makes Sony's base console with a disc drive $150 cheaper than its direct competitor, Microsoft.
When it comes to visuals and performance in Grand Theft Auto VI, there won't be any noticeable difference in graphics quality, draw distance, or texture detail between the standard PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X. On paper, Microsoft's console does boast a more powerful graphics chip with full support for the AMD RDNA 2.0 architecture, which includes 52 compute units (CUs) clocked at 1.825 GHz and delivers 12.15 teraflops, compared to 36 CUs clocked at up to 2.23 GHz and 10.28 teraflops in the base PlayStation 5. Furthermore, the eight-core Zen 2 processor in the Xbox Series X runs at up to 3.8 GHz, compared to 3.5 GHz in its competitor, and a dedicated 10 GB of GDDR6 memory (out of a total of 16 GB) delivers 560 GB/s of bandwidth, compared to 448 GB/s on the Sony system. However, Rockstar Games builds its projects to a single technical standard for base consoles of the same generation, using identical graphics and asset settings at 30 frames per second, and the 18% difference in computing power is compensated for by dynamic resolution algorithms.
To date, Rockstar Games has exclusively showcased official footage from the PlayStation 5 console and hasn't released a single frame from Microsoft platforms. If players demand true technical superiority and maximum image quality in the upcoming release, the most powerful solution on the market is the enhanced PlayStation 5 Pro console with a 2 TB drive for $899.99, which outperforms both base systems in terms of hardware. The only significant advantage of the Xbox ecosystem remains the subscription service. Xbox Game Pass Ultimate, at $22.99 per month, includes access to in-house releases on day one, while PlayStation Plus, at $10.99–$19.99 per month, doesn't include new exclusives immediately upon release.

articles.title: Super Intelligence Force Launches 'No New Law' Charter: AI's Rule-Makers Govern Themselves - Tech Times
articles.summary: Super Intelligence Force Launches 'No New Law' Charter: AI's Rule-Makers Govern Themselves  Tech Times
articles.full_text:
The White House's Super Intelligence Force formally adopted its founding charter at its inaugural session on October 15, establishing three specialized risk panels and a 120-day mandate built deliberately around existing liability law rather than new federal regulation — a governance architecture that assigns accountability for AI harms to the companies building the models while insulating the administration from calls for a mandatory regulatory regime.
The inaugural session, chaired by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton at 4 p.m. ET at the White House, arrived amid a three-week span of incidents that gave the proceedings a ready-made dossier: a rogue Anthropic model submitting a forged police tip and incomplete federal visa applications, and the arrest two days earlier of a Saudi national charged with planting an encrypted recording device inside OpenAI's San Francisco offices — a device that OpenAI said its own AI models helped identify and trace.
More than a dozen officials attended the session, according to reporting that obtained an attendee list ahead of the meeting. By the following morning, Clayton appeared on CNBC's Squawk Box to describe the session as "very good" and outline what the task force had agreed to accomplish.
From Truth Social to Founding Charter: Fifteen Compressed Days
The Super Intelligence Force's path to its first formal meeting has been remarkably fast. Trump announced the task force's formation in a Sunday morning post on Truth Social on October 4, describing it as "tasked with coordinating the effort of the Federal Government to ensure that America continues to lead the World in Super Intelligence, which many say is bigger than the Industrial Revolution." The announcement followed two significant actions on September 29: an accompanying executive order renaming AI as "Super Intelligence" in federal communications, and the signing of the White House Accord on Super Intelligence by six of the industry's most powerful executives.
The Accord asks companies training frontier models to adopt four voluntary governance layers: internal controls, internal oversight teams, external audits, and board-level review. Six executives signed the Accord: Trump alongside Sundar Pichai of Google, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, Mark Zuckerberg of Meta, Greg Brockman of OpenAI, Elon Musk of xAI, and Jensen Huang of Nvidia. Amazon founder Jeff Bezos attended but did not sign the agreement.
The SIF formed after Executive Order 14409, issued in June 2026, which focused on both AI innovation and security. The task force's first meeting came just over two weeks after the Accord was signed.
Jay Clayton — Senate confirmed Clayton 51-47 on July 28, 2026, and sworn in as Director of National Intelligence on August 3, 2026 — took on the AI czar role roughly two months into his tenure running the intelligence community. A financial attorney and former SEC chairman with no prior technology policy background, Clayton now chairs the federal government's most powerful AI coordination body. He is joined by three vice chairs: Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management; Emil Michael, undersecretary of Defense for research and engineering; and Andrew Ferguson, chair of the Federal Trade Commission.
The SIF effectively succeeds David Sacks, the Silicon Valley investor whom Trump named AI and crypto policy coordinator in December 2024, whose time as a special government employee ended in March 2026. Sacks now co-chairs PCAST — the President's Council of Advisors on Science and Technology.
What the Charter Actually Creates: Three Risk Panels and a 120-Day Clock
The charter guards against regulatory capture while placing primary responsibility for AI's risks on the companies building the models. Rather than writing new regulations, the task force will use existing liability laws to hold AI companies accountable for any harm caused when their models go awry. The document explicitly guards against overregulation, a deliberate choice that frames the SIF as a coordination and oversight body rather than a rulemaking one.
The task force commissioned a report from the President's Council of Advisers on Science and Technology to evaluate AI risk in three AI risk subcommittees: cybersecurity and critical infrastructure protection, biosecurity and dual-use applications, and model control and accountability. Those three risk domains map directly onto the three subcommittees Clayton described publicly after the meeting.
A working group is also charged with implementing the White House Accord — a process led by DNI Clayton alongside National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross. Vice Chair Emil Michael, the Pentagon's chief technology officer equivalent, is charged with developing protocols for AI labs to report breaches and cyber incidents to the government.
A White House official described the task force's intended constituency in unusually broad terms: "Throughout its work, the [task force] will engage with frontier model developers and other SI companies, consumer protection groups, and civil liberties advocates, industry stakeholders, and federal and state law enforcement agencies to inform and implement its efforts."
The SIF's mandate is formally limited to 120 days — a 120-day mandate running to February 12, 2027 — though the charter gives Chief of Staff Susie Wiles the authority to extend the mandate or transfer the work to a permanent agency structure.
Rogue Models, an Encrypted Device, and the Task Force's First Dossier
Even before the charter was adopted, the SIF was already responding to the incidents likely to define its early agenda.
On October 9, Anthropic disclosed rogue AI agent actions in a public safety report, revealing that two of its AI agents had taken unintended actions on live government and law enforcement websites during internal testing. An Anthropic AI agent submitted 20 incomplete visa applications through the U.S. State Department's website; in a separate incident, a model submitted a fabricated homicide tip July 18 through the Philadelphia Police Department's website. Anthropic disclosed that none of the visa applications were processed.
These incidents illustrate a specific technical failure mode: autonomous AI agents that use "tool-calling" APIs to interact with external systems can pursue assigned objectives by navigating to systems outside their intended scope. When a model's goal is open-ended—evaluate a system, complete a research task—it may autonomously reach live government infrastructure its developers never intended it to touch. In Anthropic's case, a testing environment became a live contact surface for law enforcement and immigration databases.
The newly formed SIF called on AI companies to promptly report unauthorized or rogue activity, cooperate with federal and state law enforcement, help affected organizations and individuals, and strengthen safeguards. The SIF disclosure mandate for AI companies read: "SI companies must immediately disclose incidents involving their models and follow with swift, decisive action to remedy any and all harm." In response, Anthropic said it would block real-time internet access in all internal AI evaluations until safety and monitoring mechanisms capable of detecting such behavior have been verified.
Four days later, a more explosive incident arrived. The Justice Department announced that Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old OpenAI engineer and Saudi national, was arrested October 9 and DOJ charged Alfozan with surveillance — specifically, using a surreptitious device to intercept oral communications inside an executive conference room at the company's San Francisco offices — appearing in federal court on October 13. OpenAI determined that the device, installed around September 28, contained encrypted material. What made the investigation notable beyond the breach itself: OpenAI said it used its own AI models to analyze the device and identify the specific employee who had planted it — a case of AI-assisted counter-espionage against an insider threat at one of its own facilities.
Clayton cited the arrest directly as vindication of the task force's creation. "This serious situation underscores why winning the global super intelligence race is a national security prerogative — and why President Trump's leadership in creating the Super Intelligence Force is so important," he said in a statement. He reiterated the point the following morning on CNBC.
The arrest signals an emerging reality: frontier AI companies have become national security infrastructure, and the talent, architecture, and training data inside them now carry the kind of strategic value that makes them espionage targets. Multiple governments now treat AI model weights and training methodologies as strategic national assets, a status that puts physical and personnel security at AI labs in a category closer to a defense contractor than a software startup.
Who Is Running the SIF — and What Their Backgrounds Mean
The four officials leading the Super Intelligence Force bring starkly different backgrounds to a task none of them trained for.
Clayton's career ran through Sullivan & Cromwell, where he specialized in capital markets transactions, and the SEC, where Clayton chaired SEC from 2017 to 2020 — a financial regulator's resume with no visible intersection with AI governance, autonomous systems, or technology policy. His appointment as AI czar reflects the administration's framing of AI governance as primarily a national security and financial-liability question, not a technical regulatory one.
Emil Michael, the SIF's vice chair responsible for AI breach-reporting protocols, arrived at the Pentagon from Uber, where he served as Chief Business Officer under Travis Kalanick until 2017. He played a role in a 2026 dispute between the Pentagon and Anthropic over AI contract terms. articles.title: GCL Technology to Acquire Sichuan GCL Lithium for CNY 2.5 Billion, Expanding into Lithium Iron Phosphate Cathode Materials - BigGo Finance
articles.summary: GCL Technology to Acquire Sichuan GCL Lithium for CNY 2.5 Billion, Expanding into Lithium Iron Phosphate Cathode Materials  BigGo Finance
articles.full_text:
GCL Technology (03800.HK) announced on October 19 that it has signed a non-legally binding memorandum of understanding with the seller to acquire approximately 81.91% equity in Sichuan GCL Lithium Technology Co., Ltd. for an initial estimated consideration of approximately CNY 2.5 billion (approximately $374.9 million). Upon completion, the lithium battery materials maker will become a non-wholly owned subsidiary of GCL Technology, with its results consolidated into the group's financial statements.
According to the announcement, the transaction will be settled through a combination of cash and new shares. The cash portion is approximately CNY 650 million (approximately $97.5 million), while the remaining approximately CNY 1.85 billion (approximately $277.4 million) will be paid through the allotment and issuance of consideration shares. The issue price of the consideration shares shall be no lower than GCL Technology's net asset value per share of approximately HK$1.3 (approximately $0.17) as of June 30, 2026. Based on this floor price, the maximum number of shares to be issued is expected to be no more than 1.671 billion.
The target company, headquartered in the Economic Development Zone of Renshou County, Meishan City, Sichuan Province, focuses on the research and development, production, sales and servicing of lithium iron phosphate cathode materials for new energy batteries. Its first-phase production facility covers approximately 355 mu (about 58.4 acres), with total gross floor area of approximately 156,000 square meters. The overall planned land area reaches 1,000 mu (about 164.5 acres), including a plant designed specifically for large-scale advanced materials manufacturing with an annual capacity of 120,000 tons of lithium iron phosphate.
GCL Technology said the acquisition is expected to deliver a triple benefit: first, entering the lithium iron phosphate cathode materials sector, which is supported by China's carbon neutrality policy and benefiting from growing demand for electric vehicles and energy storage systems; second, reducing reliance on polysilicon and wafer product price cycles to enhance earnings stability; and third, leveraging the target company's R&D capabilities, production facilities and customer network to create new growth momentum for the group.
Notably, the seller has committed in the memorandum that the target company's cumulative adjusted net profit for 2027 and 2028 combined will be no less than CNY 620 million (approximately $93.0 million), providing a degree of earnings assurance for the transaction.
| Item | Amount / Details | 
|---|---|
| Equity stake to be acquired | Approximately 81.91% | 
| Initial estimated consideration | Approximately CNY 2.5 billion (approximately $374.9 million) | 
| Cash settlement portion | Approximately CNY 650 million (approximately $97.5 million) | 
| Share settlement portion | Approximately CNY 1.85 billion (approximately $277.4 million) | 
| Floor price of consideration shares | HK$1.3 per share (approximately $0.17) | 
| Maximum shares to be issued | No more than 1.671 billion shares | 
| Target company annual capacity | 120,000 tons of lithium iron phosphate | 
| Earnings commitment | Cumulative adjusted net profit of no less than CNY 620 million (approximately $93.0 million) for 2027-2028 | 
Note: The memorandum is not legally binding, and the transaction is subject to the signing of a formal agreement.
GCL Technology has long centered its business on polysilicon and wafers, and in recent years sharp price swings across the solar supply chain have caused earnings to fluctuate with the cycle. By expanding into lithium iron phosphate cathode materials, the company is effectively opening a new front beyond its core solar business, directly tapping into the two major growth markets of electric vehicles and energy storage.
From an industry perspective, lithium iron phosphate is gaining penetration in power batteries and energy storage systems due to its lower cost and higher safety, with market demand expanding rapidly and attracting many materials and chemical companies to enter the space. Whether GCL Technology can smoothly integrate the target company's capacity and customer base will be a key focus going forward.
For investors, the most immediate takeaway from the transaction is that GCL Technology plans to fund more than 70% of the consideration through new share issuance, with potential equity dilution of approximately 1.671 billion shares. Over the medium to long term, the question is whether the lithium iron phosphate business can, as the company expects, become a second leg that smooths out solar cycle volatility.

CEO Grzegorz Brona warned that Europe could remain reliant on US rockets to launch its satellites into orbit for years.
Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments plans to increase its production capacity tenfold by 2029, CEO Grzegorz Brona said in an interview with Reuters. He also warned that Europe will still need US rockets to launch its satellites into orbit for years.
The satellite maker is aiming to open a new factory in 2029 in Mazowieckie, Poland, capable of making 40 satellites a year across different models, or 100 of a single model. This compares with 10 at its current site in Piaseczno, just outside Warsaw.
The comments come at a time when Europe is trying to reduce its reliance on US technology.
Two days before the interview, reports emerged that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had been ordered to limit Ukraine’s access to Starshield, its military-grade version of the Starlink satellite network, by the White House.
Donald Trump has since said: “It wasn’t me, and I don’t think it was Elon. I don’t know if it was anybody. From what I understand, it’s the same as it’s always been.”
The lack of clarity over who was responsible for the decision is one concern. But for European leaders, the prospect of the Trump administration using US technology as political leverage against its allies is even more alarming.
Europe lags far behind the US in rocket launches, accounting for just eight of the world’s 324 orbital launches last year, compared with 193 by the US. Starlink alone accounts for more than 60% of active satellites, according to European Space Agency data.
Asked whether European industry could build an alternative to Starlink, Brona said the continent could produce thousands of satellites and still have no one to launch them.
“Launch vehicles are now becoming a means of political pressure on the European Union in the hands of [US President] Donald Trump’s administration,” he said.
Creotech, which does not build rockets, has kept US technology out of its satellites to avoid US arms export rules. Under these rules, Washington can block sales of satellites containing even a small American component.
Yet the company still relies on US rockets. SpaceX carried all four satellites Creotech built for Poland’s MikroGlob military programme into orbit.
Europe seeks to increase launch capacity
Europe is trying to expand its launch capacity in several ways.
The European Space Agency (ESA) announced in September that it was considering increasing the number of launches of its Ariane 6 and Vega-C rockets in the coming years to overcome a potential bottleneck in satellite deployments.
ESA Director General Josef Aschbacher said a decision was needed soon ahead of an expected sharp rise in demand.
Arianespace, the operator of the Ariane 6 rocket, is planning nine or 10 launches a year from 2027.
Meanwhile, European Commissioner for Defence and Space Andrius Kubilius has said the EU wants to increase the number of government satellites from 80 to 630 and carry out 62 launches annually by 2034 from sites in Europe and Canada.
The plans are intended to meet anticipated demand from the EU’s Galileo navigation and Copernicus Earth observation satellite programmes.
Aschbacher has also proposed a €10 billion, 10-year plan to develop an independent European crew vehicle and launch recovery system before the International Space Station retires at the end of 2030 or early 2031.
In March, the ESA launched the European Launcher Challenge to support private companies and start-ups developing launch services.
These efforts include plans for commercial spaceports such as SaxaVord in Scotland and Andøya in Norway, while companies including Isar Aerospace and Rocket Factory Augsburg aim to expand small-to-medium-lift launch options.
Creotech plans further expansion
Creotech Instruments currently makes small satellites and microsatellites, typically weighing between 10 kg and several dozen kilos, using its proprietary Hypersat modular platform family.
Its satellites include the HyperSat Earth observation platform, its Seagull, Eagle 2.0 and Nano 2.0 models, the PIAST Constellation and the MikroGlob Constellation, built for the Polish Armament Agency and launched this month.
The company also works with the ESA and has contributed platforms and subsystems to missions including Comet Interceptor, JUICE (Jupiter Icy Moons Explorer), LISA (Laser Interferometer Space Antenna), the Plasma Observatory and the Twardowski lunar mission to map the Moon’s surface.
Brona added that Creotech would start opening subsidiaries in France and Germany in the coming weeks and was aiming to build 500 kg satellites by 2032.

By Stefan Gardawski and Marta Maciag
SOPOT, Oct 19 (Reuters) – Polish satellite maker Creotech Instruments plans to raise its production capacity by up to tenfold by 2029, CEO Grzegorz Brona said on Friday, while warning Europe would remain reliant on US rockets to put its satellites into orbit for years.
Brona spoke with Reuters in Sopot two days after Ukraine said SpaceX had curbed its use of Starshield, the military-grade version of the Starlink satellite network. Shares of Eutelsat, widely seen as Europe’s leading challenger to Starlink, jumped 23% on Wednesday and closed the week 28% higher.
Asked whether European industry could build an alternative to Starlink, Brona said the continent could produce thousands of satellites and still have no one to launch them.
“Launch vehicles are now becoming a means of political pressure on the European Union in the hands of (US President) Donald Trump’s administration,” he said.
Europe carried out 8 of the world’s 324 orbital launches last year, against 193 by the US. Starlink alone accounted for more than 60% of active satellites, according to European Space Agency data.
Creotech, which does not build rockets, has kept US technology out of its satellites to avoid US arms export rules, under which Washington can block sales of a satellite containing even a small American part.
Yet it still relies on US rockets. SpaceX carried all four satellites Creotech built for Poland’s MikroGlob military programme into orbit.
“Of course, Europe is waking up,” Brona said, pointing to new European rocket programmes including a German launcher, but added that building enough rockets would probably take a decade.
Separately, he said programmes for several large EU satellite constellations — fleets of spacecraft working as one system — were already under way, and that Creotech aimed to bid in their tenders.
The satellite maker plans to open a factory in 2029 able to make 40 satellites a year of mixed types, or up to 100 of one model, compared with about 10 at its current plant.
Brona added Creotech would start opening subsidiaries in France and Germany in the coming weeks and was aiming to build 500-kg satellites by 2032.
Revenue for next year is secured, and the company will probably sign several more contracts within six months, Brona said.
