articles.title: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan Says China Is “Not That Far Behind” In Chip Manufacturing, Despite US Sanctions Blocking Its Access To EUV Machines - Wccftech
articles.summary: Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan Says China Is “Not That Far Behind” In Chip Manufacturing, Despite US Sanctions Blocking Its Access To EUV Machines  Wccftech
articles.full_text:
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan believes that China is not significantly behind the US when it comes to chip manufacturing prowess. The CEO made the remarks in an interview with Nikkei Asia, where he also discussed Intel's restructuring efforts and attempts to establish a foundry business that is on par with Taiwan's TSMC, which is the world's largest contract chip manufacturer.
Intel CEO Tan Asserts Foundry Business Can Become A Growth Driver But Stresses Patience To Do It Right
China's relationship with the US when it comes to chip manufacturing technology is the source of considerable attention. Multiple high-profile names, including Elon Musk and the head of Zeiss' semiconductor business, have shared their opinions on the matter. Musk has gone as far as to claim that China could overcome manufacturing limitations as soon as in two to three years.
On the other hand, the CEO of Zeiss's semiconductor business, believes that a 15-year lag was reasonable when it came to the latest extreme ultraviolet chip manufacturing technology.
Now, Intel's CEO Lip-Bu Tan, who is one of the most experienced executives in the industry, has shared his take on the matter. Tan was asked about the landscape of the semiconductor business in the US and China in light of the US sanctions that have prevented Chinese firms from acquiring the latest EUV machines.
In response, the Intel CEO outlined that all companies, whether they are from China or the US, have different strengths and weaknesses. Continuing with his emphasis on customer requirements being paramount for any company, Tan added that products that are the best for enterprise and for customers will end up determining who succeeds.
The Intel CEO was then asked about whether China could catch up to the US when it came to advanced chip manufacturing in five to ten years. Restrictions on China being unable to procure EUV lithography machines have made it so that the country is unable to shrink its chip circuits to improve performance and power similarly to chips made by TSMC and by Intel.
Tan's response was rather brief, as he simply commented that: "Today, I think it's not that far behind."
Chinese Firm Launda's EUV Source Boasting A 100 Hour Runtime Might Be Key Breakthrough
Tan's latest thoughts came soon after China's Landau unveiled its first EUV source prototype. The light source claims to have a runtime of 100 hours with an output of 15W. ASML's first EUV lithography machine capable of high-volume manufacturing (HVM) was the NXE:3400B, which was shipped with 150W power sources and the potential to upgrade these to 250W.
The 250W figure is important since it enabled the machines to compete on a cost and scale basis with the DUV immersion lithography systems. However, the key impressive point, as noted by a semiconductor insider, is the run time.
As EUV light sources require hitting tin droplets with carbon dioxide gas a hundred thousand times each second, running it for 24 hours is so complex that ASML redefined EUV lithography scanners' runtime definition to exclude the source's runtime.

A Russian military satellite maneuvered in "extreme proximity" of a commercial Earth-imaging satellite in recent days in the first known example an unsanctioned rendezvous in low-Earth orbit, according to the orbital intelligence company LeoLabs.
The Russian spacecraft, Kosmos 2612, "conducted a deliberate series of maneuvers toward ICEYE-X36, a US-operated commercial imaging satellite," LeoLabs said. "Kosmos 2612 closed from hundreds of kilometers away to extreme proximity to ICEYE-X36. It then maneuvered around ICEYE-X36, remained nearby for an extended period, and then began moving away."
US military officials and independent analysts have tracked Kosmos 2612 since its April launch on a Soyuz rocket from a spaceport in northern Russia. Nvidia Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang projects that the company will sell twice as many chips next year as it does this year. The outlook reflects his view of sustained global demand for artificial intelligence infrastructure.
Huang made the projection at a summit with King Charles III in Scotland on Thursday. He attributed the expected growth to rising AI investment across sectors and economies, noting that people in almost every country where Nvidia operates want to invest in AI.
Sales Volume Context
Nvidia does not disclose total chip sales volume. However, during the GTC October 2025 Keynote, Huang reported that Nvidia had shipped 6 million Blackwell GPUs over the preceding four quarters. This figure provides a baseline for understanding the scale of the company's current distribution, against which the projected doubling of sales next year can be measured.
AI Safety and Regulation
Huang attended the U.K. summit alongside representatives from Alphabet Inc.'s Google (NASDAQ: GOOG), DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic to discuss AI safety. While acknowledging safety issues, Huang pushed back against calls for a broader slowdown in AI development.
"When a product is not safe, we should hold it back and keep engineering it," Huang said. He emphasized that labs do not need new rules to ensure safety, countering narratives of an impending AI slowdown.
Long-Term Spending Outlook
Earlier this month, Huang described Nvidia as the "World’s First and Only Growth Value Stock." He positioned the company's expanding AI platform, broad customer base, and infrastructure partnerships to capture the next phase of global AI spending. Huang anticipates AI infrastructure spending to reach $3 trillion to $4 trillion by 2030.
This long-term view aligns with CFO Colette Kress’s projection of approximately 70% revenue growth for the fiscal year ending January 2028, as discussed during the company’s Q2 earnings call.
Asset Durability
Huang also emphasized the value of AI computing hardware as a financeable asset. He noted that rental prices for Nvidia’s older H100 GPUs continue to climb. This trend reinforces his view that "NVIDIA compute is fungible, durable and highly rentable," suggesting that even older hardware retains significant economic value in the current market.

The combination of Huang’s expectation for doubled chip sales and the reported shipment of 6 million Blackwell GPUs in the last four quarters highlights a massive scale of operations. While Nvidia does not report total volume, the specific disclosure of Blackwell shipments serves as a key indicator of its current production capacity and market penetration, providing context for the aggressive growth forecast.

articles.title: Faces Up to 20 Years: California CEO in Nvidia Server Case - Grit Daily News
articles.summary: Faces Up to 20 Years: California CEO in Nvidia Server Case  Grit Daily News
articles.full_text:
Greg Lui, a California technology company owner, was arrested in a case alleging that more than $300 million in Nvidia chips reached buyers in China through false paperwork and shipments routed through Malaysia and Singapore. Federal prosecutors say the alleged exports took place from 2023 to 2024 and involved high-end servers.
The Department of Justice announced the charges on October 1. The source report says Lui, also known as Yiu Kong Lui, was arraigned and made his initial court appearance that day. The allegations place the case among recent federal actions involving executives accused of misconduct, including a CEO payroll-tax indictment.
How the Alleged Nvidia Shipments Took Route
Prosecutors allege that Lui and unidentified co-conspirators first exported the chips to Malaysia and Singapore. They then allegedly shipped them onward to Chinese buyers, including the Chinese government. The source report says those destinations were used because the restrictions did not apply there.
Authorities say paperwork described permissible end users and destinations that did not require an export license, although the chips allegedly went to China. The charges concern export-controlled computer servers. The reported charges name Lui and unidentified co-conspirators.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli, of the Central District of California, said the defendant allegedly used false documents and third-country shipments to move more than $300 million in controlled servers to China. His statement frames the alleged route and paperwork as central to the prosecution’s case.
Charges and Potential Sentence
The Justice Department charged Lui with one count of conspiracy to violate the Export Control Reform Act and the Export Administration Regulations. The other counts are one count of outbound smuggling and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering.
If convicted of all charges, Lui could face up to 20 years in prison, according to the report. That is a potential sentence, not a conviction or sentence already imposed. The source gives no response from Lui or his representatives to the allegations.
The criminal case sits alongside other disputes and prosecutions involving technology businesses and their leaders. Grit Daily has also reported on a startup equity claim and a separate technology procurement case. Those cases are distinct and do not establish facts about Lui’s case.
Federal Agencies Are Investigating
The FBI, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security Office of Export Enforcement, and the Defense Criminal Investigative Service are jointly investigating. The source does not describe further planned court dates or a timetable for the investigation.
Special Agent in Charge John E. Helsing of the Defense Criminal Investigative Service’s Western Field Office said preventing illegal exports of controlled technology is important to protecting national security. Helsing said such technologies provide core advantages to U.S. forces and that enforcement helps keep them from parties that may threaten the United States.
The allegations also come amid other reported export-control cases. The source says nine people were indicted in Taiwan last month over the illegal export of Nvidia B300 GPUs to China. It describes that matter as part of a series of cases, without saying it is connected to Lui or his alleged co-conspirators.
The United States and its allies have placed broad export restrictions on some AI chips and related hardware, the report says. China has said the restrictions strengthened its domestic AI ecosystem, while demand for Nvidia GPUs in China has contributed to a market for smuggled hardware, according to the report. The next concrete step in Lui’s case will depend on the federal prosecution and investigation now underway.

articles.title: Why Starlink is so important for Ukraine - DW.com
articles.summary: Why Starlink is so important for Ukraine  DW.com
articles.full_text:
Few technological systems have played such an important role in the war in Ukraine as Starlink, central to the communications, reconnaissance and drone operations of the Ukrainian armed forces. There are currently widespread concerns that Elon Musk's satellite internet service in Ukraine may be restricted or even switched off. In recent days, Kyiv has repeatedly reported disruptions and restrictions affecting its use.
How Starlink enables communications
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022, Ukraine has made extensive use of the satellite internet service, which is operated by the US company SpaceX. With it, military personell can continue to communicate and exchange data, even when infrastructure has been destroyed or cellphone networks are down.
According to the Center for Security Studies (CSS) at ETH Zurich, around 50,000 Starlink terminals were in use in Ukraine in 2025. These are the system's specialised receiving and transmitting devices, which enable communications on the battlefield. They are also used to relay orders between command levels and receive drone footage.
The importance of the Starlink network can in part be explained by events at the beginning of the war. According to a CSS analysis, the KA-SAT satellite system previously favored by Ukraine was targeted in a cyberattack just hours before Russia's invasion. Starlink quickly became a vital alternative.
Starlink and Starshield: civilian versus military use
When discussing current affairs, the terms "Starlink" and "Starshield" are often used interchangeably.
However, Starlink is SpaceX's commercial satellite internet service, whereas Starshield is specifically designed for governmental and military use. While based on the same technological infrastructure, it is designed for security and defense applications.
This distinction matters, because the latest reports of restrictions seem to primarily concern systems used for military purposes. Elon Musk recently stated that Starshield systems are controlled by the US government, whereas Starlink is a commercial service operated by SpaceX.
The role of Starlink in drone warfare
Alongside communications, Starlink is mainly used for drone operations. The system provides an internet connection for ground, naval and aerial drones.
This connection means video footage can be transmitted almost in real time, while drones can be controlled over long distances. Ukraine uses these systems for reconnaissance and attacks deep behind enemy lines.
According to ETH Zurich, images and GPS coordinates of Russian positions are also transmitted via these communication channels. The data is sent to artillery units and used to coordinate operations.
What throttling Starlink would mean
According to Ukrainian media reports, on Tuesday night, SpaceX temporarily introduced a speed restriction for Starlink terminals in Ukraine, limiting terminals in motion to a speed of about 160 kilometers per hour (100 mph).
Such a restriction has direct consequences for fast-moving Ukrainian drones, some of which travel at speeds of up to 300 kilometers per hour (186 mph). If the connection to the drone is lost, live video footage can no longer be transmitted, and the systems can no longer be controlled in real time. The drones effectively have to continue their mission while flying blind.
Restricting or even shutting down a Starlink network would therefore not only make communication more difficult. It would also affect Ukrainian drone operations, and other military activities.
More than just satellite internet
However, Starlink and its military counterpart, Starshield, are only one essential component of Ukraine's defense system. Ukraine also receives reconnaissance data from western partners, including information about Russian air attacks, missile launches, troop movements and anti-aircraft positions, as well as potential routes to avoid them.
This information helps with air defense and offensive operations. Without this intelligence, it would be significantly harder for Ukraine to carry out long-range drone operations against targets in Russian territory.
The two elements are particularly effective when combined. Reconnaissance data provides information about potential targets and routes, while Starlink ensures that this data can be quickly relayed to units.
This is why reports that the US is limiting access to its reconnaissance data are as worrying as the possibility that Starlink might be throttled. Other NATO countries, such as the United Kingdom and France, can also provide reconnaissance data, but not to the extent as the United States.
Strategic dependence
Europe has several alternatives to Starlink, including Eutelsat/OneWeb. However, their ability to match Starlink's performance in wartime conditions has not yet been tested on a large scale.
The recurrent concern about possible restrictions makes clear that satellite communications have become a central component of Ukrainian defense. And while relying on a single provider simplifies operations, it also shows how dependent modern armed forces have become on private technology companies. Experts say this marks a fundamental change in warfare.
Meanwhile, Ukraine's successful use of Starlink has helped the system to achieve global recognition.
This article has been translated from German.

articles.title: SpaceX's $40 Billion AI Gambit: Nvidia Chips, a Spectrum Shopping Spree and the Coming Q3 Verdict - ad-hoc-news.de
articles.summary: SpaceX's $40 Billion AI Gambit: Nvidia Chips, a Spectrum Shopping Spree and the Coming Q3 Verdict  ad-hoc-news.de
articles.full_text:
SpaceX is no longer a rocket company that happens to launch things. It is becoming an orbital infrastructure giant — and the price tag for that transformation is coming into focus.
At the center of the shift is a financing package that would make most aerospace balance sheets buckle. According to reports from Reuters and Bloomberg, SpaceX has been in talks to raise $40 billion to buy Nvidia AI chips, split between roughly $30 billion in investment-grade bonds and $10 billion in bank loans. The funding is not yet finalized, but the structure alone signals intent: this is borrowing against the future of computing in space.
From Launch Pads to Data Streams
The strategic logic runs deeper than hardware. Pairing space-based data centers with a dense satellite constellation could erect entry barriers that rivals would struggle to surmount. It also demands extraordinary financial discipline from management, because the sums involved dwarf anything the commercial space industry has attempted before.
The technical ambitions match the financial ones. Starlink confirmed it placed the first 26 V3-generation satellites into orbit at the end of September. Longer term, the company envisions operating up to 100,000 Starlink satellites, plus as many as one million more for its AI project, Starmind.
On the ground — or rather, in the airwaves — SpaceX is buying its way into direct-to-cell service. It agreed roughly two weeks ago to acquire Grain Management's nationwide spectrum portfolio, including the 800 MHz low-band frequencies, for about $8 billion in cash, according to media reports. The deal still requires approval from the US telecom regulator, the FCC.
A Backbone That Keeps Firing
None of this would matter without the launch cadence that underpins it. On Thursday, a Falcon 9 carried the classified USSF-481 mission for the US Space Force. Two days earlier, a Dragon freighter delivered more than 6,300 pounds of cargo to the International Space Station on the CRS-35 mission. No private player matches that tempo — or that closeness to government and military customers.
That proximity cuts both ways. When civilian satellite networks factor into matters of war and peace, the operator lands squarely between state interests. Debate over restricting Starshield access for Ukraine and over speed throttling illustrates how narrow the line is between commercial service provider and geopolitical actor. Can a private company permanently shield itself from the demands of state power while remaining its most important transporter?
Fusion Talk and a Sober Market
Into this mix came pure speculation: Barclays analysts floated a possible merger between Tesla and SpaceX, suggesting an announcement could arrive as early as late October or early November. It is analyst conjecture, not a confirmed transaction, and investors would do well to tune it out.
The market, meanwhile, has turned noticeably cooler. The stock closed Friday at €129.96, down 1.9% on the day and 33% below its 52-week high. A broad selloff in US tech, with semiconductor names hit hardest, added to the gloom.
The October 20 Test
Hard evidence about the company's operating health is due soon. On Tuesday, October 20, SpaceX will report third-quarter 2026 financial and operating results after the US market close — a report that amounts to a reckoning for shareholders.
The numbers must show whether cash flow from the regular launch business can carry the astronomical infrastructure plans, or whether the cost of orbital dominance is leaving the company financially exposed. The vision of a planet-spanning AI network in Earth's orbit is compelling. It also requires patience, deep pockets and a high tolerance for risk — and proof that the refinancing of all that expensive hardware goes through without a hitch.

articles.title: Smashed Quantum Computing Record Raises Stakes for Bitcoin Security - Bitcoin News
articles.summary: Smashed Quantum Computing Record Raises Stakes for Bitcoin Security  Bitcoin News
articles.full_text:
Quantum computing firm Quantinuum has announced a major breakthrough in error correction, achieving a record 99.9995% logical fidelity that it says strengthens its path toward a commercially viable, fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029. The advance comes amid mounting concerns that increasingly powerful quantum machines could eventually undermine the cryptography protecting bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies.
Smashed Quantum Computing Record Raises Stakes for Bitcoin Security
Key Takeaways
- Quantinuum achieved a record 99.9995% logical fidelity, reducing quantum error rates tenfold from September.
- The breakthrough advances Quantinuum’s goal of delivering a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029.
- Progress raises concerns for Bitcoin security, as powerful quantum computers could eventually break cryptographic protections, accelerating calls for quantum-resistant upgrades.
Quantum Accuracy Is Rapidly Improving
Quantinuum said Monday that its Helios quantum computer achieved a logical error rate of just five errors per million operations, a tenfold improvement over its previous record set in September. The company claims the result is also 100 times better than the best published result using competing quantum hardware architectures, previously reported by Google Quantum AI.
The breakthrough addresses one of quantum computing’s biggest challenges: keeping calculations accurate despite the extreme sensitivity of quantum bits, or qubits, to errors. Unlike conventional computers, quantum systems require sophisticated error-correction techniques to reliably perform complex calculations.
Quantinuum achieved the result using a technique known as a “color code,” which combines multiple physical qubits into more reliable logical qubits. The company’s researchers also demonstrated that errors declined exponentially as they increased the level of protection, with each tested increase reducing the remaining logical errors by a factor of 12.
The results build on Quantinuum’s September breakthrough, which used a different error-correction method on the same Helios hardware.
“We’ve crossed the threshold necessary for exponential improvements in accuracy, reinforcing our path to Apollo and how we can help users unlock commercial value from quantum at scale,” said Quantinuum CEO Rajeeb Hazra, in a statement.
The company said its latest achievement brings error-correction performance into the target range for Apollo, its planned universal fault-tolerant quantum computer expected by 2029.
Robin Blume-Kohout, co-director of Sandia National Laboratories’ Quantum Performance Lab, who was not involved in the research, called the achievement a significant milestone. He said the findings suggest a scaled-up system could achieve useful fault-tolerant computing with fewer than one million physical qubits.
The results nevertheless concern a specific error-correction benchmark rather than a demonstration of a large-scale, general-purpose quantum computer. Significant engineering challenges remain before such systems can execute complex algorithms reliably.
Bitcoin’s Quantum Threat Comes Into Focus
The announcement follows a separate breakthrough announced by Google Quantum AI last week, as researchers demonstrated a technique called “magic state cultivation” that reduced errors by a factor of 40. The research achieved 99.99% logical fidelity in producing specialized quantum states needed for certain advanced computations.
As Bitcoin.com News reported, Google’s progress has renewed concerns about “Q-Day,” the hypothetical point at which quantum computers become powerful enough to break widely used cryptographic systems.
Earlier this year, Google researchers estimated that breaking the elliptic-curve cryptography used in Bitcoin’s digital signatures could require fewer than 500,000 physical qubits, roughly 20 times fewer than some previous estimates.
The research also outlined a theoretical scenario in which an advanced quantum computer could derive a bitcoin private key from an exposed public key in approximately nine minutes.
Researchers estimated that about 6.9 million BTC—nearly one-third of the total possible supply of bitcoin—could be potentially vulnerable because their public keys have already been exposed, including funds held in older wallet formats and reused addresses.
Although Quantinuum’s latest breakthrough does not demonstrate any capability to crack Bitcoin’s cryptography, it represents progress toward the reliable quantum computation that could eventually make such attacks feasible.
The developments have intensified discussions about preparing cryptocurrency networks for a post-quantum world. Fidelity Digital Assets has warned that exposed Bitcoin public keys could become vulnerable, while Coinbase has highlighted the technical challenges of transitioning the Bitcoin network to quantum-resistant cryptography.
Potential defenses include new digital signature schemes, but implementing them could require substantial changes to Bitcoin’s infrastructure, including larger signatures, wallet upgrades, and coordination across the decentralized network.
A particularly difficult issue involves dormant bitcoin holdings whose owners may be unable to migrate their funds to quantum-resistant addresses.
For now, no existing quantum computer is capable of breaking Bitcoin’s cryptographic protections. But with Quantinuum targeting 2029 for its fault-tolerant Apollo system and Google making rapid progress on related technologies, the race to develop quantum-resistant cryptocurrency infrastructure is taking on greater urgency.

articles.title: The three big debates around music and generative AI - completemusicupdate.com
articles.summary: The three big debates around music and generative AI  completemusicupdate.com
articles.full_text:
There have been many discussions over the last few years regarding music and AI - and especially in relation to generative AI models that output music, and which have been trained using existing human-created recordings and songs. These models pose numerous different questions for music creators and the music industry, some legal, some commercial and some ethical.
Some of these questions relate to issues where there is quite a lot of consensus and unity within the music industry, with artists, musicians, songwriters, composers, studio producers, collecting societies, and both major and indie record labels and music publishers, more or less aligned. But some relate to issues where there is a growing divide between different stakeholder groups within the music community.
Given all the many different questions and issues, navigating the music and AI discussions can get confusing. To help, CMU has organised many of these questions and issues into three distinct strands - the big three music and AI debates.
This Friday, CMU’s Chris Cooke will join a panel to discuss music and AI at Un-Convention in Manchester, and ahead of that discussion here he provides an overview of each of the big three debates, running through the key questions being asked, and recent trends and developments.
Big debate #01: The obligations of AI companies
On the input
When training a generative AI model to output music, an AI company needs to copy a large quantity of existing music, both songs and recordings, into a training dataset. It then analyses that data to build its model. Additional copies may be made and manipulated during the subsequent training process.
Copyright law gives copyright owners control over who can copy their works, which means in theory the AI company must get permission from all the relevant copyright owners before making these copies. In the case of a recording of a song, that would include the owners of the separate copyrights in the recording and the song or composition.
However, many AI companies did not secure permission from rightsholders before they trained generative AI models, instead arguing they could make copies of existing content, like music, without rightsholder consent because of ‘copyright exceptions’ or ‘fair use’.
Copyright law in some countries includes an exception covering text and data mining - often called TDM exceptions - which allows third parties to make copies of content for that purpose without getting permission from rightsholders. Many AI companies argue that applies to AI training, so - if they do their training in those countries - they don’t need to get rightsholder permission.
US copyright law has a similar principle called ‘fair use’ - if use of a copyright protected work is ‘fair’ permission is not required. Many AI companies argue AI training is fair use.
Lobbyists for many AI companies have also been pressuring lawmakers in different countries to introduce new copyright exceptions to make it easier to use existing works in AI training without getting permission from the relevant copyright owners or creators.
The music industry is pretty much united in seeking to block attempts by AI companies to exploit existing exceptions or the fair use principle, or to introduce new exceptions. The music industry - along with the wider creative industries - is adamant copyright exceptions and fair use do not - and should not - apply to AI training.
To that end, record companies, music publishers, collecting societies and individual music creators have all filed lawsuits in the US, Europe and elsewhere seeking to demonstrate - by setting legal precedents in different courts in different jurisdictions - that AI companies cannot rely on exceptions or fair use when copying music into training datasets in order to train generative AI models.
Among the AI companies fighting lawsuits filed by the music industry are Suno, Udio, Anthropic and Open AI. All of these cases continue to work their way through the litigation process.
There have also been moves to clarify or change copyright law so that - even if AI companies can exploit exceptions in a small number of countries to train models without getting rightsholder permission - those models cannot then be commercialised in other countries where no such exceptions exist.
On the output
Some generative AI platforms also make use of existing music on the output - for example by remixing existing songs - or exploit an artist’s voice or name on the output - by generating vocals that imitate a performer or allowing users to generate music ‘in the style’ of specific human creators.
Where this is happening by design (sometimes it happens by mistake) most AI companies accept that they need to get permission from rightsholders and/or performers.
They generally accept that when existing songs are replicated or remixed in an AI output, copyright exceptions and fair use do not apply. And if an AI output imitates an artist’s voice or is generated ‘in the style of’ an existing artist, it is likely other creator rights are also being exploited, such as personality or publicity rights, personal data rights and trademarks.
It’s actually not clear precisely how personality, data and trademark rights apply to the use of voice or name on AI outputs, and in the UK personality rights do not currently exist. To that end, there have been proposals in various countries for new digital replica rights that specifically apply to AI-generated outputs, and most of these proposals have been endorsed and supported by the music industry.
However, even where these rights are being clarified and evolved, most AI companies are more cautious when it comes to exploiting works, voices and names within the content that their models’ output.
Trends + developments
The big dispute between the music industry and the tech sector about the legal obligations of AI companies is far from over. However, some tech companies have started to negotiate licences covering AI training and outputs with music industry rightsholders.
In some cases, that’s because the AI company wants to do the right thing. Sometimes it’s because they are also streaming platforms that have existing relationships with the music industry. Sometimes it’s because they want to offer remix tools or voice cloning on the output and therefore recognise licences are required. And sometimes it’s because of legal risks.
Whether AI training is ‘fair use’ under US copyright law - meaning existing music can be used for AI training without getting permission - remains an active and very contentious legal question.
Dozens of lawsuits in the US courts, including those filed by authors, book publishers, newspaper owners and film studios, as well as the music industry, centre on the question of ‘fair use’. In the first two cases to get to trial, against Anthropic and Meta, both involving book authors and the written word, the judges accepted fair use arguments put forward by the two tech companies.
However, in the Anthropic case the judge said AI training was only fair use if the AI company got the original copies of the books it trained on from legitimate sources, and many AI companies have relied on pirated material to build training datasets.
And the judge in the Meta case said an AI company’s fair use defence might fail if a copyright owner can show the outputs of any one generative AI model cause market dilution, impacting on the commercial value of the rightsholder’s works.
So, with music, if tracks generated by an AI model could be shown to significantly reduce the commercial value of the human-created music it was trained on, the fair use argument may not apply.
These mixed-bag rulings have created legal uncertainties for AI companies. Under US law a copyright owner can sue for up to $150,000 for each work that has been wilfully infringed and most AI companies have copied millions of works without licence. This means if any one AI company ultimately loses a copyright infringement lawsuit in the US, it could be forced to pay out a trillion dollars or more in damages.
In that context, it is arguably in the interests of an AI company to sort out copyright licences now to remove that risk. And some rightsholders - including music companies - have been able to use the risk of almost unlimited damages to pressure AI companies into negotiating licensing deals.
Which creates a second big debate.
Big debate #02: The obligations of labels and publishers
On the input
Forcing AI companies to agree to licensing deals to train their models sounds like a big win for the music industry - and in many ways it is. But as record labels and music publishers begin to enter into licensing deals with AI companies to allow training with their catalogues, there are a number of new questions that are immediately posed for stakeholders within the music industry.
- Will labels and publishers seek specific consent from individual artists and songwriters before allowing their recordings and songs to be included in the AI training deals they have negotiated, given AI uses were not anticipated in any old record or publishing deals?
- How will any money the label or publisher receives from an AI company be allocated to individual recordings or songs in their catalogues? With AI training, you could possibly argue that every work is equally important so should get an equal share of the money - but is that the approach the industry is taking?
- Will recordings and songs be treated equally? With streaming, more money flows to the recording than the song, whereas with sync the two distinct rights usually earn more or less the same. Will income from AI training be split equally or in some other way?
- Once money has been allocated to any one recording or song by a label or publisher, what share of that money will be paid to the artist or writer? Record deals often have one royalty rate for streams and record sales and another higher rate for licensing deals - will the higher rat

articles.full_text:
ANSYS
Industry leader in CAE
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Battery Modeling Tools market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global battery modeling tools market is entering a decade of structural expansion as electrification across transport, energy storage, and consumer devices raises the engineering complexity of battery systems. These software platforms, which include physics-based electrochemical simulators, equivalent circuit model tools, data-driven analytics, and cloud-based digital twins, have moved from specialist research environments into core commercial engineering workflows.
The 2026 baseline reflects a market shaped by rapid battery chemistry evolution, including lithium-sulfur and solid-state concepts, and by the pressing need to shorten development cycles while improving safety and lifetime prediction. Demand is concentrated in electric vehicle battery design, where high-fidelity models reduce physical prototyping, and in grid-scale storage, where degradation and cost modeling inform investment decisions.
The competitive field combines established simulation software vendors, specialized pure-play battery modeling firms, and open-source libraries, with differentiation increasingly tied to computational efficiency, model accuracy, and integration with PLM and BMS development environments. Over the 2026-2035 forecast horizon, growth will be supported by the maturation of battery digital twins, standardization of modeling frameworks, and the spread of cloud deployment, while cost pressures and skills shortages temper the pace of adoption in smaller enterprises.
The baseline scenario for the world battery modeling tools market through 2035 assumes continued electrification investment across automotive, stationary storage, and consumer electronics, with no abrupt reversal in battery technology roadmaps. Under this scenario, the market expands at a compound annual growth rate of 12.4% from 2026 to 2035, lifting the market index to 285 by 2035 from a 2025 base of 100. Growth is front-loaded in the early years as automakers and cell manufacturers scale simulation teams, then moderates as tooling becomes embedded in standard engineering workflows and pricing competition intensifies.
The strongest demand pull comes from electric vehicle battery design, where high-fidelity physics-based models and hybrid multi-scale simulators are used to evaluate new cell chemistries and pack architectures before physical prototypes are built. Grid-scale energy storage optimization is the second major pillar, as project developers and integrators rely on degradation and lifetime models to underwrite long-duration storage assets. Consumer electronics battery life prediction remains a steady, volume-driven segment, while aerospace and stationary backup power provide smaller but high-value niches with stringent safety and reliability requirements.
On the supply side, the market is diversifying toward cloud-based delivery and subscription licensing, which lowers barriers for smaller engineering firms but pressures margins for on-premise license vendors. Restraints include the high cost of high-fidelity simulation talent, data quality limitations for emerging chemistries, and the risk that open-source libraries commoditize basic modeling functions. Overall, the baseline outlook is for sustained double-digit expansion, with the market index reaching 285 by 2035.
Electric vehicle battery design is the largest and fastest-growing end-use segment for battery modeling tools. Automakers and cell manufacturers are under pressure to shorten vehicle development cycles while improving range, safety, and cost, which makes simulation indispensable. High-fidelity physics-based models and hybrid multi-scale simulators are used to evaluate new cell chemistries, electrode designs, and pack architectures before physical prototypes are built. Through 2035, the segment's demand will be driven by the shift to solid-state and high-nickel chemistries, the need for thermal runaway prediction, and the integration of battery models into vehicle-level digital twins.
Demand-side indicators to watch include the number of new EV platforms in development, cell manufacturer capital expenditure, and the share of engineering budgets allocated to simulation versus physical testing. As EV production scales globally, modeling tools become a standard line item in battery engineering workflows, supporting sustained growth in this segment. Current trend: Rising.
Major trends: Shift toward solid-state and high-nickel chemistries requiring new model calibration, Integration of battery models into vehicle-level digital twins, Growing use of cloud-based simulation for collaborative engineering, Rising demand for thermal runaway and safety simulation, and Compression of development cycles through virtual prototyping.
Representative participants: Ansys, COMSOL, Siemens Digital Industries Software, Gamma Technologies, AVL, and MathWorks.
Grid-scale energy storage optimization is a rapidly expanding end-use segment as utilities and project developers deploy large battery systems for renewable integration and grid balancing. Modeling tools are used to forecast degradation, estimate lifetime, and optimize dispatch strategies, which directly affect project economics and warranty terms. Through 2035, demand will be supported by the growth of long-duration storage, the need to model second-life batteries, and the integration of storage into wholesale energy markets. Demand-side indicators include installed grid storage capacity, the number of storage projects reaching financial close, and the adoption of performance guarantees that rely on modeled degradation curves.
As storage assets age, operators increasingly use digital twin platforms to monitor state-of-health and optimize maintenance, creating recurring software demand beyond initial project design. Current trend: Rising.
Major trends: Growth of long-duration storage requiring new degradation models, Integration of storage into wholesale energy markets, Rising use of digital twins for operational monitoring, Second-life battery analysis for repurposing projects, and Performance guarantees tied to modeled degradation curves.
Representative participants: TWAICE, Reactive Technologies, Siemens Digital Industries Software, Dassault Systèmes, and Electro-Active Technologies.
Consumer electronics battery life prediction is a mature but steady segment driven by smartphone, laptop, and wearable makers competing on battery performance and charging speed. Equivalent circuit model tools and empirical data-driven platforms are widely used to predict runtime, cycle life, and thermal behavior under different usage patterns. Through 2035, demand will be shaped by the adoption of fast-charging technologies, silicon-anode chemistries, and the need to simulate battery behavior in increasingly compact devices. Demand-side indicators include unit shipments of consumer devices, the pace of charging standard upgrades, and the share of device makers using simulation in early design stages.
While growth is slower than in EV and grid storage, the segment provides a stable base of recurring software licenses and is increasingly served by cloud-based platforms that lower deployment costs for mid-sized device makers. Current trend: Stable.
Major trends: Adoption of fast-charging technologies requiring thermal simulation, Emergence of silicon-anode chemistries in consumer devices, Shift to cloud-based modeling platforms for cost efficiency, Integration of battery models into device-level design workflows, and Growing focus on battery longevity in product marketing.
Representative participants: MathWorks, Ansys, COMSOL, Sendyne, and Battery Design.
Aerospace and aviation battery systems represent a smaller but high-value segment where safety and reliability requirements are stringent. Modeling tools are used to simulate thermal runaway, failure propagation, and performance under extreme conditions, supporting certification and risk assessment. Through 2035, demand will be driven by the electrification of aircraft systems, the growth of electric vertical takeoff and landing vehicles, and the use of batteries in satellites and unmanned systems. Demand-side indicators include aerospace electrification programs, certification requirements for battery systems, and research and development spending in the sector.
The segment places a premium on model accuracy and traceability, which supports higher-value software licenses and consulting services. As aviation electrification advances, modeling tools will become integral to design and certification workflows. Current trend: Rising.
Major trends: Electrification of aircraft systems and eVTOL development, Stringent certification requirements for battery safety, Use of batteries in satellites and unmanned systems, Growing need for failure propagation simulation, and High-value consulting and support services.
Representative participants: Ansys, COMSOL, Siemens Digital Industries Software, AVL, and Gamma Technologies.
Stationary backup power systems, including uninterruptible power supplies and telecom backup batteries, form a stable end-use segment for battery modeling tools. Modeling is used to predict battery life under float and cycling conditions, optimize replacement schedules, and ensure reliability during outages. Through 2035, demand will be supported by the growth of data centers, telecommunications infrastructure, and resilience requirements for critical facilities. Demand-side indicators include data center capacity growth, telecom network expansion, and the adoption of lithium-ion batteries in backup applications. The segment is price-sensitive, which favors reduced-order models and cloud-based tools that offer lower total cost of ownership.

Can Cobre Panama copper mine run for 25 years without growing?

The mine, run by First Quantum Minerals, was closed in 2023 after it was ruled unconstitutional following protests against its operation. articles.title: SpaceX Starlink Trust Issues: Why Governments Are Concerned - Business Outreach Magazine
articles.summary: SpaceX Starlink Trust Issues: Why Governments Are Concerned  Business Outreach Magazine
articles.full_text:
SpaceX has spent years proving that a private company can build a satellite network large enough to become important infrastructure.
That success is creating a new problem.
Governments are now asking what happens when the same privately operated network becomes essential to military communications, emergency response or other national-security systems—and access is later restricted.
Recent disruption involving Starshield services used by Ukraine has brought those questions back into focus. The issue is no longer whether SpaceX Starlink technology works. It clearly does.
The harder question is who ultimately controls it when the service becomes strategically important.
Ukraine Put the Dependence Problem Into Full View
Starlink became deeply embedded in Ukraine’s communications environment after the conflict with Russia began.
Satellite connectivity proved useful because terrestrial infrastructure could be damaged, jammed or otherwise disrupted.
Over time, Starlink and the military-focused Starshield service became important for communications, surveillance and drone-related operations.
That dependence looked very different when connectivity was reduced.
Reuters reported this month that restrictions affecting Starshield disrupted some Ukrainian military operations, including drone missions.
The episode exposed a simple weakness.
If a country’s battlefield communications depend heavily on infrastructure controlled outside its borders, changes to that infrastructure can immediately become a national-security issue.
The Argument Over Who Ordered the Restrictions Matters
The situation is complicated by disagreement over who was responsible.
Reuters reported that an instruction to limit aspects of Starshield service originated from within the White House, citing US and Western officials.
Elon Musk has said operational limits affecting Starshield are controlled by the US government.
Public accounts around authorisation and responsibility have nevertheless remained contested.
That distinction is important because the concern is not simply whether SpaceX independently switched something off.
The broader Starshield trust issue exists even when a government directs the restriction.
A country relying on foreign satellite infrastructure may still find that access is affected by decisions made somewhere else, under a legal and political system it does not control.
Satellite Connectivity Has Become Strategic Infrastructure
Starlink began as a broadband product.
That description now feels incomplete.
A global satellite network can connect homes, businesses, ships, aircraft and remote communities. The same infrastructure can also support defence operations, government systems and emergency communications.
Once that happens, reliability takes on a different meaning.
A streaming customer losing internet access for 20 minutes is inconvenient.
A military unit losing connectivity during an operation is something else entirely.
That is why satellite digital sovereignty is becoming a much larger policy question.
Governments increasingly need to think about who owns the network, where control systems sit, which laws apply and whether service continuity is contractually guaranteed.
SpaceX Still Has a Huge Technological Advantage
None of this removes what SpaceX has achieved.
Starlink operates at a scale few competitors can match.
SpaceX controls its own launch capability, manufactures satellites and has built an enormous low-Earth-orbit network. That vertical integration allows it to deploy and replace capacity more quickly than many rivals.
The company is also expanding into direct-to-phone connectivity.
Earlier this month, SpaceX announced an agreement to acquire an 800 MHz spectrum portfolio in the United States for about $8 billion, strengthening its plans for Starlink Mobile.
The technical ambition is getting larger, not smaller.
The problem is that greater capability also creates greater scrutiny.
Governments May Start Asking for Stronger Guarantees
A commercial customer normally accepts terms of service.
A government relying on satellite communications for critical infrastructure may eventually demand much more.
That can include guaranteed availability, clear rules around service restrictions, independent oversight and specific procedures governing when access can be altered.
Countries may also insist on greater operational visibility rather than depending entirely on decisions made by the network provider or another government.
Those requests could increase the cost and complexity of Starlink government contracts.
They could also slow market entry in countries where regulators already have national-security concerns.
For SpaceX, trust could therefore become as important as coverage or bandwidth when bidding for sensitive work.
India Shows Why This Question Is Broader Than Ukraine
India’s approach to Starlink offers a useful example.
SpaceX has received important approvals related to satellite communications, but commercial operations still depend on additional regulatory, security and spectrum requirements.
Indian authorities have been examining concerns around network control, data, security compliance and how satellite services operate during sensitive situations.
The government has not banned Starlink.
It has, however, been cautious about allowing commercial service before the security framework is settled.
That caution predates the latest Ukraine episode, but the episode gives regulators another real-world case to consider.
India Is Not Evaluating Starlink Alone
Starlink is also not the only company facing satellite regulation in India.
Reliance Jio and Bharti-backed satellite ventures are moving through their own regulatory processes.
India’s communications ministry has said satellite operators are being assessed through the country’s security and spectrum framework and has rejected claims that the process is designed to favour one operator.
That matters because the broader issue is not SpaceX versus one Indian rival.
It is how India wants satellite connectivity to fit into national infrastructure.
A foreign provider can offer technology and coverage that would take years to recreate locally.
The trade-off is the degree of dependence policymakers are willing to accept.
Countries May Decide One Network Is Not Enough
The most likely response may not be to reject foreign satellite systems entirely.
It may be diversification.
A government could use commercial networks while maintaining separate domestic or allied capabilities for the most sensitive functions.
Military organisations already think in terms of redundancy because relying on one communication route creates a single point of failure.
The same logic can apply to satellites.
If one network is jammed, restricted or unavailable, another should be able to take over.
That could create more demand for sovereign satellite networks and competing low-Earth-orbit systems rather than leaving critical operations dependent on a single provider.
The Trust Question Will Follow SpaceX Into New Markets
VARINDIA describes the current situation as a global trust crisis for SpaceX.
The eventual impact will depend on how governments respond.
Some may demand stronger contracts. Others may invest more heavily in domestic alternatives. Many are likely to keep using Starlink while avoiding complete dependence on it.
SpaceX still holds a formidable technical position.
Its satellite network is large, launch capability is difficult to match and its direct-to-device plans could extend Starlink into another huge communications market.
But the company is increasingly entering areas where technology is only one part of the purchase decision.
For SpaceX and Starlink, the next challenge is proving not just that the network can connect almost anywhere.
It is proving that governments can understand, predict and trust what happens to that connection when the stakes are highest.

articles.full_text:
Quantinuum Sets World Record for Quantum Computing Accuracy
Quantinuum sets record with 99.9995% accuracy on Helios quantum computer.
Quantinuum announced a record-breaking logical accuracy of 99.9995% on its commercial quantum computer Helios. This equates to five errors per million operations and is ten times better than the company’s previous result achieved just a month earlier.
Quantinuum has achieved a major industry breakthrough that solves a critical error-correction bottleneck and validates our path to delivering a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2029.
We’ve announced a new world record for quantum error correction, achieving 99.9995% logical fidelity on our Helios commercial quantum computer using our error-correction architecture.
Equivalent to just five errors in a million operations, the result is 10× better than our previous record achieved just last month and 100× better than the best published result on any other hardware modality.
The study also demonstrated a record 12× reduction in logical errors as code distance increased, a critical step toward scalable fault tolerance.
These successive breakthroughs using different codes on the same commercial hardware demonstrate how Quantinuum’s flexible error-correction architecture and highly accurate trapped-ion technology work together to enable exponential improvements in accuracy, with performance now within the target range for Apollo, our first universal fault-tolerant quantum computer planned for 2029.
Learn more: https://t.co/I1RpLxeo55
— Quantinuum (@QuantinuumQC) October 19, 2026
The record was achieved using a well-known color code in Quantinuum’s proprietary error-correction architecture. This result is 100 times better than the best published result on any other hardware platform, which was achieved by Google Quantum AI on a superconducting system. As code distance increased, logical errors decreased exponentially, with each tested increase reducing remaining errors by 12 times.
Why It Matters
The company claims to have surpassed the threshold necessary for exponential accuracy growth, with performance now within the target range for Apollo, a universal fault-tolerant quantum computer planned for release by 2029. According to CEO Rajib Hazra, the result demonstrates the presence of both the error-correction architecture and the trapped-ion technology needed for universal fault tolerance.
Independent expert Robin Blume-Kohout from Sandia National Laboratories noted that the logical qubit is nearly 100 times superior in quality to its constituent physical qubits. A scaled version of the system, in his estimation, could achieve the required reliability with fewer than a million physical qubits.
In September 2026, the company set a record on the same Helios using a different code, Helix. The comparison revealed a trade-off: Helix uses 10 physical qubits per logical qubit, while the color code uses up to 37 but results in fewer errors. This allows for code selection tailored to specific tasks as the company progresses toward fault tolerance.
Earlier, in April, the U.S. Department of Energy announced plans to create a fully functional fault-tolerant quantum computer for scientific calculations within three years.

articles.title: AST SpaceMobile Rises 4% as Europe's Largest Carriers Explore Joint Satellite Spectrum Bid; SpaceX and Rocket Lab Edge Higher - 24/7 Wall St.
articles.summary: AST SpaceMobile Rises 4% as Europe's Largest Carriers Explore Joint Satellite Spectrum Bid; SpaceX and Rocket Lab Edge Higher  24/7 Wall St.
articles.full_text:
Europe's four biggest wireless carriers just signed on to explore a joint satellite spectrum bid, and one space stock is surging while its biggest rival watches from the sidelines.
Europe’s four largest wireless carriers are moving toward a coordinated satellite spectrum push, and AST SpaceMobile (NASDAQ:ASTS) is central to the effort. AST SpaceMobile stock is up 4% to $42.24 in early trading, outpacing the space names around it. The gain follows a company press release stating that its carrier partners signed a letter of intent to explore a potential joint bid for mobile satellite services spectrum.
Meanwhile, SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX | SPCX Price Prediction) stock is at $147.45, up 0.9%, a smaller gain than AST SpaceMobile stock. Rocket Lab (NASDAQ:RKLB) shares are up 2%, also trailing AST SpaceMobile stock.
Carrier Spectrum Letter Lifts AST SpaceMobile
AST SpaceMobile stated that its mobile network operator partners, which it described as Europe’s four largest carriers, signed the letter of intent to explore a potential joint bid for mobile satellite services spectrum. Through its regional joint venture, Satellite Connect Europe, the company is providing European-operated ground infrastructure that links its BlueBird satellites to the carriers’ core networks.
This letter covers only a potential spectrum bid, and AST SpaceMobile’s release names no financial terms. It stops short of a commercial agreement, so it adds no signed revenue yet.
AST SpaceMobile Runs Ahead of the Space Group
The Procure Space ETF (NASDAQ:UFO) is up 1%, trailing AST SpaceMobile stock by a wide margin. AST SpaceMobile accounted for 4% of the fund’s net assets as of July 31, and the ETF also held shares of SpaceX and Rocket Lab. Across the wider market, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) is up 0.49%.
This spread marks the rally as specific to AST SpaceMobile stock. SpaceX runs its own direct-to-cell service through Starlink, which competes with the carriers’ satellite plans.
BlueBird Fleet Backs the Carrier Pitch
AST SpaceMobile has 13 BlueBird satellites in orbit and is targeting about 45 by early 2027. Its carrier partners together cover more than 3 billion subscribers, giving a European spectrum push a large potential customer base.
Ground infrastructure is moving in parallel at AST SpaceMobile. The company has nearly 50 gateways in various stages of completion, installation and planning across five continents.
Caution still fits for AST SpaceMobile, given its latest results. In its Q2 2026 report, the company posted revenue of $31.52 million, missing expectations, along with a loss of $0.77 per share under generally accepted accounting principles that also fell short.
Management at AST SpaceMobile confirmed revenue guidance of $150 million to $200 million for the year and expects quarterly sales to climb as the year progresses. Following its recent convertible notes offering, the company’s pro forma liquidity tops $3.7 billion, which gives it room to keep building satellites. Those funds sit alongside a signed revenue backlog of roughly $1.3 billion from commercial partners and U.S. government awards.
AST SpaceMobile’s European Carrier Partners Hold the Next Step
AST SpaceMobile’s next step depends on the carriers’ spectrum bid. Investors can watch for whether that bid becomes a commercial agreement that turns the letter of intent into signed revenue.
The upside case for AST SpaceMobile rests on carriers moving toward European spectrum, while the downside points to no financial terms, a Q2 revenue miss and competition from SpaceX. Until a commercial agreement is reached, bullish holders should keep their exposure moderate.

- Quantinuum and The University of Western Australia (UWA) sign MOU to help prepare Australia’s workforce and innovation ecosystem for the hybrid quantum-AI-HPC computing era
- Quantinuum will provide UWA-affiliated researchers, students and entrepreneurs with access to its full-stack quantum computing ecosystem, including Helios, the world's most accurate commercial quantum computer1
- Collaboration will focus on developing quantum applications for sectors critical to Australia's economy, including critical minerals, energy, agriculture, and healthcare
BROOMFIELD, Colo., and PERTH, Australia—October 5, 2026—Quantinuum (NASDAQ: QNT), a leading quantum computing company, today announced the signing of a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with The University of Western Australia (UWA) to advance Australia’s quantum capability by expanding access to advanced quantum computing, developing quantum talent, and accelerating the development of practical applications that integrate quantum computing, AI, and high-performance computing (HPC).
Through the collaboration, UWA-affiliated researchers, students, and entrepreneurs will gain cloud-based access to Quantinuum's full-stack quantum computing platform, including Helios, the company's latest-generation quantum computer. The partnership is designed to provide hands-on experience with advanced quantum technologies while creating new opportunities to explore how quantum computing, artificial intelligence, and high-performance computing can work together to address complex real-world challenges.
The organisations will also explore opportunities to expand UWA's Quantum and AI research ecosystem through a university-wide quantum computing applications centre that would bring together academic, industry, and government stakeholders to identify and develop high-value use cases in critical sectors for Australia’s economy, including critical minerals, energy, agriculture, and healthcare.
"Australia has set an ambitious vision for quantum, and it is making meaningful progress toward turning that vision into reality thanks to leadership from institutions like UWA," said Marvin Lee, Quantinuum’s Singapore-based Country Leader. "Together, we're bringing our full suite of capabilities, from world-leading hardware and software to application expertise and ecosystem programs, to develop practical quantum applications and hybrid workflows that will prepare Australia for the quantum era and support the nation's future prosperity."
Beyond providing access to advanced quantum systems, the partnership aims to help build the technical capabilities and innovation networks needed to support Australia's long-term quantum ambitions. Through engagement with Quantinuum programs such as Q-Net and the Startup Partner Program, researchers, developers, and entrepreneurs will have opportunities to access training, collaborate with peers across the global quantum ecosystem, and accelerate the development of quantum-enabled solutions.
Working alongside UWA researchers and industry stakeholders, Quantinuum experts will help evaluate candidate use cases, establish technical benchmarks and assess hybrid workflows that integrate quantum computing, artificial intelligence, and high-performance computing.
Professor Jingbo Wang, founder and Director of UWA’s Research Centre for Quantum Information, Simulation and Algorithm (QUISA), said the partnership built on UWA’s strengths in quantum computing research.
“Through co-design with potential end users and quantum computing hardware providers, this initiative will create new opportunities for UWA researchers, students and industry partners, while strengthening interdisciplinary collaboration across the University. We look forward to exploring all the opportunities this will bring for our researchers as well as student pathways, internships and workforce training initiatives,” Professor Wang said.
“Access to leading quantum technologies helps Australian researchers, students and companies build capability and understand where quantum can deliver real value,” said Petra Andrén, CEO of Quantum Australia. “Collaborations like this create opportunities to develop skills, test applications and connect research with industry challenges. Australia has strengths across the quantum technology stack. Access to the best capabilities, both here and internationally, will help translate those strengths into economic and community benefit.”
The partnership reflects a shared commitment to ensuring Australia remains not only a source of quantum discovery, but a place where quantum technologies are put to work solving real-world challenges and creating economic value.
About Quantinuum
Quantinuum is a leading quantum computing company offering a full-stack platform designed to make quantum computing deployable in real-world environments. The company has commercially deployed multiple generations of trapped-ion based quantum systems built on the well-established QCCD architecture, which it has implemented with novel designs and capabilities to achieve the industry’s highest accuracy levels based on average two-qubit gate fidelity. Quantinuum has active engagements with market leaders across pharmaceuticals, material science, financial services, and government and industrial markets, as well as academic and research institutions globally. The company has a global workforce of approximately 800 employees, including top scientists and researchers. Over 70% of its technology team holds PhDs or Master’s degrees. Quantinuum’s headquarters is in Broomfield, Colorado, with additional facilities across the United States, United Kingdom, Germany, Japan, Qatar, and Singapore. For more information, please visit www.quantinuum.com.
About UWA
For more than 110 years, The University of Western Australia has been a place where ambition meets action. As the state’s first and leading university, we inspire students, researchers and partners to create meaningful change and tackle the world’s most pressing challenges. Located on the banks of the Derbal Yerrigan (Swan River), our main campus stands on land where kaartdjin (knowledge) has been shared for tens of thousands of years. This enduring legacy of learning shapes our diverse global community of more than 28,000 students from 100 countries, connected to a powerful network of over 150,000 graduates making an impact worldwide. Ranked in the global top 100 (QS 2027) and a member of the prestigious Group of Eight, UWA is recognised for excellence in teaching, research and industry collaboration. From sustainability and health to technology and communities, our work drives real-world outcomes.
At UWA, impact starts here. For more information visit: uwa.edu.au

articles.title: European telecoms groups join forces to challenge Elon Musk’s Starlink - Financial Times
articles.summary: European telecoms groups join forces to challenge Elon Musk’s Starlink  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter.
Four of Europe’s largest telecoms groups are exploring launching their own satellite mobile services to challenge the dominance of Elon Musk’s Starlink, in a move that could further inflame transatlantic tensions over the communications technology.
Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone said on Monday that they had signed a letter of intent to explore a potential joint bid for radio wave spectrum that would enable them to provide “direct-to-device” satellite mobile services in Europe.
The move comes amid an intensifying geopolitical dispute over satellite telecommunications services.
In May, the European Commission proposed reserving the part of its spectrum band that allows smartphones to connect directly to satellites for European players. The so-called 2 GHz frequency band is currently used by two American companies, Viasat and EchoStar, whose licences expire next year.
The proposal has become a transatlantic tension point. Last week, the US ambassador to the EU told the FT that European companies would face “devastating” retaliation if the bloc did not change its proposal, which would be prejudicial against US companies such as Starlink.
The Commission’s plans have been fiercely criticised by SpaceX, which operates the Starlink platform. The tech giant warned the move risked poorer connectivity in Ukraine where Starlink has been critical to civilian and military communications since Russia’s full-scale invasion.
Starlink has been at the centre of controversy this month after its services were disrupted in Ukraine amid tensions between US President Donald Trump and his counterpart in Ukraine, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The European companies’ joint satellite initiative has been privately applauded by the bloc’s officials, according to several people involved in the discussions. The EU is pushing to reduce Europe’s heavy reliance on core digital infrastructure provided by suppliers outside the bloc.
The initiative would mean the companies establishing the necessary ground infrastructure, or base stations, needed for satellite connectivity.
However, instead of developing their own satellite constellation, they would partner with an existing provider, which is yet to be selected.
This could pose challenges for the proposal, with most satellite constellations being operated by US or Chinese companies. French satellite operator Eutelsat has developed a large-scale constellation but the company is far behind Starlink, which has more than 11,000 satellites in orbit.
Goldman Sachs analyst Andrew Lee said the move was a “reassuring reminder to investors that European operators see satellite as a companion technology to their domestic networks and that European authorities wish to carve out satellite-ready spectrum for European players”.

articles.summary: Washington Threatens “Devastating” Consequences as Europe Moves to Curb Starlink  UNITED24 Media
articles.full_text:
- Category
- World
Washington Threatens “Devastating” Consequences as Europe Moves to Curb Starlink
The United States has warned that European companies could face “devastating” retaliation if the European Union moves forward with plans to restrict access to satellite communication frequencies for American companies, including Elon Musk’s SpaceX, as Brussels seeks to reduce its dependence on foreign technology.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the Financial Times on October 18, US Ambassador to the EU Andrew Puzder warned that Washington could take retaliatory measures against European businesses if the bloc introduces regulations favoring domestic satellite operators over American competitors.
Asked whether European companies should be concerned about potential retaliation, Puzder said they “should be wary that it could happen and it would be very devastating for those companies,” citing the size of the US market.
The warning follows a European Commission proposal to reserve part of the radio spectrum used for direct satellite-to-smartphone communications for European operators. The measure would limit access to certain frequencies for non-EU companies, including American and Chinese satellite providers.
SpaceX has strongly criticized the proposal, warning that restrictions could negatively affect connectivity in Ukraine, where its Starlink satellite network has played a critical role in civilian and military communications since Russia launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022.
At the same time, the dispute comes amid renewed concerns about Ukraine’s reliance on American satellite communications infrastructure.
On October 14, Ukrainian forces reported restrictions affecting SpaceX satellite terminals installed on high-speed drones. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry subsequently confirmed that terminal operations had been restored, although reports of additional disruptions continued.
On the frontline, Starlink supports communication between Ukrainian military units, the transmission of battlefield intelligence, and drone operations. Interruptions to the service can disrupt coordination and limit the effectiveness of unmanned systems used for reconnaissance and strikes.
Beyond military operations, satellite connectivity also provides backup communications for emergency responders and essential civilian services, particularly when Russian attacks damage telecommunications infrastructure or disrupt electricity supplies. Any prolonged loss of connectivity could complicate rescue operations and emergency coordination.
The proposed changes form part of a broader European effort to strengthen technological independence and reduce reliance on American companies for critical infrastructure. European policymakers have increasingly raised concerns about dependence on US technology amid uncertainty surrounding President Donald Trump’s policies.
Puzder acknowledged Europe’s right to protect sensitive government information but argued that regulatory measures should not undermine American companies to benefit European competitors.
“You don’t make European companies more competitive by making US companies less competitive,” Puzder told the Financial Times.
The ambassador also criticized the EU’s broader approach to regulating major technology companies, questioning whether enforcement of the Digital Markets Act was intended to promote competition or generate revenue through multibillion-euro fines imposed on American businesses.
Beyond satellite communications, Brussels is pursuing additional measures to strengthen its domestic technology sector, including proposed sovereignty requirements for providers of sensitive cloud services.
Puzder warned that excessive regulation could discourage American investment in Europe and weaken cooperation between the two economies. He urged Washington and Brussels to work together on artificial intelligence and quantum computing rather than impose additional restrictions on each other’s technology companies.
The European Commission defended its proposal, saying it “incentivises the entry into the market and diversification of EU suppliers, while remaining open to non-EU operators.”
Meanwhile, the European Union is developing its own secure satellite communications network, IRIS², designed to provide government and commercial connectivity through a constellation of 290 satellites. The project is expected to become operational by 2030 as part of the bloc’s efforts to strengthen its space-based communications capabilities.
