articles.title: Russian military satellite closes from 200 miles to 3 miles of US radar satellite aiding Ukraine — astronomer says it may be the first unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit - Tom's Hardware
articles.summary: Russian military satellite closes from 200 miles to 3 miles of US radar satellite aiding Ukraine — astronomer says it may be the first unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit  Tom's Hardware
articles.full_text:
A Russian military satellite, Cosmos 2612, has closed to roughly 3 miles, from a previous distance of more than 200 miles, of the U.S.-owned radar satellite that operates in a fleet that supports Ukraine, Axios reports. The unapproved rendezvous in low Earth orbit, which astronomer Jonathan McDowell says may be the first of its kind, raises alarm in the West. The position change, which was likely not an accident as fuel is scarce, is probably a provocation and an attempt to spy on the satellite.
LeoLabs said in a statement Friday that the movement “appears to be a deliberate approach” toward ICEYE-X36, with uncertain intent and behavior that “warrants continued monitoring.” Roughly 3 miles is too close for comfort in satellite terms: there is no strict legal limit on how close satellites can get, but countries generally keep at least 6 miles (9.7 km) apart, University of Mississippi space law professor Aaron Brynildson told Axios. The approach was made without the owner’s consent, and Russia hasn’t said what the military satellite carries.
Some clues may come from the target’s operational purpose. ICEYE-X36 is a synthetic aperture radar (SAR) satellite which can image through cloud cover and at night. It was launched in March 2024 on a SpaceX Falcon 9. It’s registered to ICEYE US, the U.S. arm of the Finland-founded company. The satellite, which is in a roughly 545 km (339 mi) sun-synchronous orbit, is part of a fleet that has supplied Ukraine with information since 2022. This includes a deal earlier this year with a customer in Ukraine’s defense ministry, but a Ukrainian official told Axios it’s unclear whether ICEYE-X36 itself supports the country; ICEYE and the Defense Department declined to comment.
In May, the majority of the six military satellites Russia launched in April via a Soyuz-2.1b, Cosmos 2609–2614, shifted their orbits about 0.8 degrees to match X36’s orbital plane. Cosmos 2609 passed within 2.5 km (1.6 mi) on May 26. Cosmos 2612, on the other hand, drifted off X36’s plane by about 0.24 degrees by Sept. 30, up to about 28 km side to side, according to Greg Gillinger, a space analyst with Integrity ISR.
Then, Cosmos 2612 made separate burns from Sept. 30 through Oct. 16 to match altitude, eccentricity, and orbital period, Dutch satellite tracker Marco Langbroek wrote. By Saturday night, he estimated from public orbital data, it was within “a few hundred meters or possibly (much) closer.”
These movements appear deliberate and cost a lot of fuel, which the Center for Strategic and International Studies calls “a limited resource on a satellite.” Close-proximity work can be benign, it says, but policymakers should assume the Russian satellite “could take an action that threatens the commercial satellite,” and the U.S. and Europe should decide how to respond to any hostile act in space and make a statement on the decision. Back in July 2020, Russia’s Cosmos 2543 released an object at up to 186 m/s (416 mph) relative to itself, an action which was condemned by the U.S. and U.K.
Intent was less clear earlier this year, when McDowell told Meduza the orbital data showed no sign of the stable, close distance that tracking ICEYE-X36 would require. Now, he says it is an unapproved meeting and is not alone. Gillinger says the setup “removes any remaining doubt for me that Cosmos 2612 is interested in ICEYE X36.” Langbroek adds that “I was skeptical” at first but now calls it “completely non-consensual,” though he cautions it would be difficult to pin any X36 failures on 2612’s actions.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
In a Reuters report less than two weeks ago, ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski said the company moved its satellite after May, only to draw more Russian maneuvers, which Germany’s Space Command head, Maj. Gen. Michael Traut, described as “chasing.” Belinda Marchand, chief scientist at U.S. space intelligence firm Slingshot Aerospace, added that the moves may have been meant for surveillance, to prepare for future interference, or to signal capability. Western officials reportedly describe such trailing as a way to gather intelligence and test the West’s tolerance.
No statement from Russia is on record. Gillinger also told readers to “watch Cosmos 2611 and 2613, whose planes are converging on ICEYE X37’s,” with crossings expected around Nov. 6 and Nov. 15.

articles.title: Europe launched 8 orbital rockets last year, can it rival Starlink? - The News International
articles.summary: Europe launched 8 orbital rockets last year, can it rival Starlink?  The News International
articles.full_text:
CEO Grzegorz Brona says Europe could build thousands of satellites and still depend on US launchers
Europe carried out 8 of the world's 324 orbital launches last year. The US managed 193. For Poland's Creotech, that gap, not satellite building, is the real obstacle to a European rival to Starlink.
CEO Grzegorz Brona told Reuters in Sopot on Friday that the company plans a 2029 factory able to build 40 satellites a year of mixed types, or up to 100 of a single model. Its current plant makes about 10.
Creotech will also open its subsidiaries in France and Germany over the coming weeks, and it aims at manufacturing 500-kg satellites by 2032. Brona stated that the revenue for the next year is secure, and he expects to get other contracts within the next six months.
According to Brona, launchers have turned into “a political weapon” in the hands of the Trump administration. Creotech does not manufacture rockets, and Brona claims that “Europe can produce thousands of satellites without any launchers.”
Creotech ensures that no American technology is used in its satellites because if even one American part exists in the satellite, Washington can stop its sale. However, SpaceX put all four satellites manufactured by Creotech for Poland’s MikroGlob military programme into space.
While pointing to the new European rocket programmes, including the German launcher, Brona claims that manufacturing enough rockets will take almost a decade.
The comments came two days after Ukraine said SpaceX had curbed its use of Starshield, the military version of Starlink. Eutelsat, seen as Europe's leading Starlink challenger, jumped 23% on Wednesday and ended the week 28% higher.
Starlink alone accounts for more than 60% of active satellites, according to European Space Agency data.

articles.title: SpaceX throttled Starlink in Ukraine. Neither Trump nor Elon Musk wants to own the decision. - Yahoo Finance
articles.summary: SpaceX throttled Starlink in Ukraine. Neither Trump nor Elon Musk wants to own the decision.  Yahoo Finance
articles.full_text:
As Russia tries to make Ukrainian cities unlivable with relentless bombing ahead of another war-torn winter, either the US president or the world's richest person — or both — appear to be hindering Ukraine's ability to defend itself.
President Trump and SpaceX (SPCX) founder Elon Musk are reportedly involved in the apparent restriction in Ukraine of SpaceX's Starlink satellite communications network and Starshield, its subscription service designed for military use.
"Elon Musk approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," The Telegraph reported on Friday, citing four sources familiar with the discussions, adding that Trump "agreed."
Starlink, a global broadband internet service delivered from space, is a core part of SpaceX's business. Starlink has more than 13 million subscribers worldwide, and SpaceX is now moving to challenge legacy wireless carriers.
SpaceX stock rose 1% before the bell on Monday.
Ukraine uses both Starlink and Starshield for a variety of offensive and defensive purposes, including communication, logistics, live drone feeds, radar, targeting, and intercepting jet-powered Russian drones.
The Telegraph reported that after the Ukrainian capital endured a barrage of Russian jet-powered drone attacks with diminished capabilities for air defense, Musk became "alarmed about the possibility of adverse consumer reaction in Europe."
On Wednesday, Ukraine's former defense minister posted on X, tagging Musk, and asked for his support: "Removing Starshield's speed limit entirely is now critical for Ukraine's defense."
Musk responded, asserting that limits on speed or usage of Starshield "are decided by the US military and ultimately POTUS" and that Starlink "is limited to civilian or defensive activities."
"He tweeted out that he was innocent and that it was the US administration that did it," an unnamed source told The Telegraph. "The reality is that they were both in it."
On Friday, Trump told reporters that "it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon."
On Sunday, speaking to NBC's Meet the Press, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said that it's the "opinion of our generals, of our government, and of course [also my] opinion, that it was a message from [the] American government to limit the speed. And technically, SpaceX did it."
Zelenskyy also openly wondered why the decision was made and said the service had not been restored to normal speed.
"Just give us back Starlink," he said. "And of course, if they will not, we will survive and we will not stop to defend [Ukraine] even without it. But why? I can't understand. For what? What are the reasons to limit us? Not to defend ourselves?"

articles.title: ByteDance MediaTek Deal 2026: Nvidia's $3.5B Partner Pivots - Memeburn
articles.summary: ByteDance MediaTek Deal 2026: Nvidia's $3.5B Partner Pivots  Memeburn
articles.full_text:
TL;DR
- ByteDance is close to a deal to buy custom AI chips from MediaTek for its data centers.
- It would be MediaTek's second major AI chip customer, after Google. Terms aren't public yet.
- Nvidia invested $3.5 billion in MediaTek in August, so its partner may now ease its own grip.
- ByteDance already buys from Qualcomm and gets limited Nvidia H200 chips under US export rules.
- ByteDance may spend up to $70 billion on AI infrastructure this year, double last year.
ByteDance, the company behind TikTok, is reportedly close to a deal to buy custom AI chips from MediaTek, the Taiwanese firm best known for the processors inside budget and mid-range Android phones. It’s a big deal now because US export rules keep Nvidia’s best chips out of Chinese hands, and ByteDance needs huge amounts of computing power to run its AI chatbot and the features inside its apps. Here’s what’s being negotiated, why a phone chipmaker is suddenly in the data center business, and the twist that puts Nvidia in an awkward spot.
What’s on the Table
The talks are in the final stages, according to people familiar with the negotiations, but nothing is signed. Neither company has confirmed the deal, and the number of chips and the price haven’t been disclosed.
MediaTek would supply ASICs, short for application-specific integrated circuits. An ASIC is a chip built for one customer’s specific workload, unlike a GPU (graphics processing unit) from Nvidia, which is a flexible chip that can handle almost any AI job. Think of a GPU as a Swiss Army knife and an ASIC as a chef’s knife. The chef’s knife does fewer things, but it does its one job faster and with less effort.
If it goes through, ByteDance becomes MediaTek’s second major custom AI chip customer, after Google.
Wait, Isn’t MediaTek a Phone Chip Company?
It is, and that’s what makes this interesting.
MediaTek’s Dimensity chips power a huge share of the world’s Android phones, especially in the $150 to $500 range. But phone sales are flat, and AI data centers are where the money is growing. So MediaTek has been quietly rebuilding itself.
- It doubled its 2026 target for AI chip sales to about $2 billion.
- It wants roughly 15% of an $80 billion custom AI chip market by 2027.
- Its first big data center project is widely understood to be tied to Google’s TPUs, Google’s in-house AI chips.
Then, on August 31, Nvidia invested $3.5 billion in MediaTek through convertible bonds, a type of loan that can later turn into shares. As part of their partnership, MediaTek’s customers can use Nvidia’s NVLink Fusion, a high-speed connection that lets custom chips plug into Nvidia’s data center systems.
Keep that detail in mind. It’s the key to the twist later on.
ByteDance’s Three-Lane Chip Plan
ByteDance isn’t swapping one supplier for another. It’s building three lanes at once.
| Supplier | What ByteDance gets | Status | 
| Nvidia | H200 GPUs | US-approved but heavily limited; first shipments arrived this summer | 
| Qualcomm | Custom AI chips (“millions” reported) | Deal reported in May 2026 | 
| MediaTek | Custom AI chips | Talks in final stages | 
The Nvidia lane is the narrowest. The US approved H200 sales to selected Chinese firms in December 2025, with Washington taking a 25% cut. But Beijing wants most of those chips kept in Hong Kong rather than mainland China, and early H200 deliveries to ByteDance and Tencent were only about 10,000 units each, a tiny fraction of what was licensed.
Custom chips are a workaround. Under current US rules, Chinese firms can work with chip designers as long as the finished chips stay below set computing-power limits. That doesn’t make them free of scrutiny, though. Custom AI chips aren’t automatically exempt from export controls, and Washington can tighten the rules at any time.
Here’s how we see it. ByteDance isn’t trying to beat Nvidia on raw speed. It’s buying insurance. If one lane closes, two others keep its data centers running.
Why ByteDance Needs So Much Computing Power
ByteDance is one of the biggest AI users in the world, and most people outside China don’t realize it.
Its chatbot Doubao handles more than 180 trillion tokens a day, a figure ByteDance shared in June that it says is over ten times higher than a year earlier. A token is a small chunk of text, roughly three-quarters of a word, and it’s the unit AI companies use to measure how much work their models do.
That workload lands on data centers, and the spending shows it:
- ByteDance may spend up to $70 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026, more than double last year.
- That could reach $100 billion in 2027.
- It took out a $30 billion loan in September to help pay for it.
Most of that demand is inference, the work of running a trained model every time someone asks it a question. Training builds the model once. Inference happens billions of times a day. ASICs shine at inference because they’re tuned for repetitive work and use less power per answer. Other giants are making the same move, from Amazon’s push into loosening Nvidia’s grip to Alibaba’s effort to stop paying GPUs to sit idle.
The Twist: Nvidia’s Money, Nvidia’s Rival
Six weeks after Nvidia put $3.5 billion into MediaTek, MediaTek may help one of China’s largest AI buyers rely less on Nvidia. It sounds like a contradiction. We don’t think it fully is.
Nvidia knows big tech companies want their own chips. Google, Amazon and Meta have all built them. So Nvidia’s bet is that if custom chips are coming anyway, it would rather they plug into Nvidia’s networking and server systems through NVLink Fusion than into a rival’s. In that world, Nvidia sells the highway even if it doesn’t sell every car.
Whether that applies to ByteDance is less clear. Export rules limit which Nvidia technology can go into Chinese data centers, so MediaTek’s chips for ByteDance may not connect to Nvidia hardware at all. That’s the part we’ll be watching most closely if the deal is announced.
Either way, the bigger signal is that MediaTek, Qualcomm and Broadcom are all fighting for the same custom-chip work that used to belong to Nvidia’s GPUs alone.
This isn’t the end of Nvidia’s dominance. It’s the start of a world where the biggest AI users split their orders among several suppliers, and where companies you associate with phones end up running the AI behind your feed.
FAQs
How much water and power do AI data centers use?
A lot, and it’s growing fast as companies like ByteDance expand. Water consumption makes up much of the cooling a data center needs, and AI companies use the most.
Can I run AI models on my own computer instead?
Yes, smaller models run well at home. You can check how much RAM and VRAM you need for local AI explains which model sizes fit on a laptop, a gaming PC, or a desktop workstation.
Is TikTok adding more AI shopping features?
It is. TikTok’s new AI shopping assistant answers product questions using brand-supplied information and adds in-app checkout, though it’s still in limited US testing with advertisers.
Are tech companies sharing AI models with rivals?
More than you’d expect. Google recently put Claude inside Gemini, so the company choosing your AI model can profit whether you use its own model or a rival’s.

articles.title: AI Governance at UNGA81: Safety, Security and the North-South Divide - Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI)
articles.summary: AI Governance at UNGA81: Safety, Security and the North-South Divide  Bloomsbury Intelligence and Security Institute (BISI)
articles.full_text:
By Martyna Chmura | 19 October 2026
Summary
- Artificial intelligence (AI) became a central issue at the 81st United Nations General Assembly (UNGA81), with 128 delegations addressing it, compared with only five four years earlier, highlighting growing concern over who controls AI development, benefits from it and bears its risks.
- UNGA81 exposed competing approaches to AI governance: the United States (US) prioritised continued innovation and rejected global oversight, the European Union (EU) backed a UN-centred regulatory architecture, while China and many Global South states emphasised inclusion, national participation and narrowing the digital divide.
- AI safety is increasingly linked to international security and the North-South divide, as developing states warn that frontier-AI safeguards could become technological gatekeeping if countries controlling advanced models, computing power and data also determine global rules.
Context
AI moved from a specialist technology issue to a major question of international governance during UNGA81 in September 2026. The UN President of the General Assembly, Khalilur Rahman, noted that 128 delegations addressed AI, more than those discussing human rights or climate change. Rahman argued that governance must be human-centred and prevent a new divide in which a small number of countries and companies control data, computing power and rules.
Positions nevertheless diverged. US President Donald Trump rejected a global framework to govern AI, arguing that the United States should prioritise the growth and leadership of “superintelligence” while relying on domestic oversight to address its risks. By contrast, European Council President António Costa called for an accountable, transparent and regulated architecture, with the UN playing a central role through the Global Digital Compact, Independent International Scientific Panel and Global Dialogue on AI Governance. China called for a “people-centred” approach, narrowing the digital divide and increasing the Global South's voice.
Implications
The growing focus on AI safety and security demonstrates a rising trade off between limiting risks and preserving the technology’s development potential. AI’s use in military decision-making, cyber operations and information environments strengthens the case for safeguards against cross-border harms, including human oversight and accountability in high-stakes applications. However, a security-first approach could also legitimise restrictions that constrain access to beneficial applications in healthcare, agriculture and public services. Nigeria’s warning against “surrender[ing] our technological future to paranoia” reflects a broader concern that risk management should not become a barrier to innovation. The central challenge is to distinguish safeguards against specific harms from restrictions that could limit AI’s wider development and use.
Despite these differences, cooperation is likely to be more achievable through targeted safeguards than a comprehensive global regulatory framework. While the UK aims to advance common AI principles during its G20 presidency, Finland and Norway have called for international control of frontier AI models. Such initiatives could support convergence on testing, transparency, human oversight and accountability in high-risk applications, without requiring uniform domestic regulation. However, progress towards shared standards should not be mistaken for agreement on their scope or enforcement. Disagreement over government intervention, frontier AI development and national autonomy will likely continue to constrain efforts to establish binding international rules.
The prospects for cooperation are further complicated by the global divide in AI capabilities. Countries with advanced computing infrastructure, investment and technical expertise are better positioned to develop standards and meet demanding safety requirements, while less-resourced states risk becoming rule-takers or facing barriers to participation. Pakistan’s warning that slowing frontier AI must not become “a new form of gatekeeping” captures this concern. India’s emphasis on the right of each nation to shape its own AI ecosystem also reflects the importance of technological autonomy. Effective multilateral governance will therefore require not only inclusive rule-making but also investment in the infrastructure, skills and institutional capacity needed to implement standards and benefit from AI.
Forecast
- Short-term (Now - 3 months)
  - Global South states will likely press for technology transfer and capacity-building, while resisting safety measures perceived as restricting access.
  - International initiatives will likely prioritise practical cooperation on high-risk AI, including testing, transparency and human oversight, rather than comprehensive binding rules.
- Medium-term (3 - 12 months)
  - Regulatory fragmentation will likely persist as states and regional organisations develop standards reflecting different approaches to innovation, security and national sovereignty.
  - The May 2027 UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance will likely increase pressure for interoperability and common principles, although agreement on enforceable international obligations will remain limited.
- Long-term (>1 year)
  - International AI governance will likely develop around shared principles and technical safeguards for high-risk applications, without necessarily producing a unified global regulatory regime.
  - Comprehensive, binding limits on frontier AI capabilities are unlikely while major powers continue to prioritise technological leadership and strategic advantage.

articles.title: Three reasons why AI is not conscious and perhaps never will be
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 19 October 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03313-7Large language models can mimic thought and feeling with uncanny skill. But evidence from neuroscience suggests that intelligence alone is not enough for subjective experience.
articles.full_text:
Artificial-intelligence systems such as large language models (LLMs) can exhibit behaviour that seems strikingly intelligent. This has led many people, including some experts, to wonder whether these systems could have some form of consciousness — the capacity for subjective experience. However, we think that existing AI systems are not conscious, and that, along current trajectories of development, they are not likely to become conscious. Greater clarity about whether AI could become consciousness will be crucial as society grapples with the challenges posed by this increasingly powerful technology.
Can AI ever be conscious? The question stems from a misconception
Several prominent scientists, including biologist Richard Dawkins and AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton, have argued that AI systems might already be conscious. And earlier this year, AI company Anthropic in San Francisco, California, published research claiming to have identified computational signatures of a form of consciousness in its Claude model1.
Whether AI models can ever be conscious is not merely a philosophical question. It has practical implications. For instance, if AI systems were conscious, they might experience distress and pain, similar to how people do. Then should countless new conscious entities that might experience suffering be allowed to proliferate? Perhaps not surprisingly, some people are already calling for ‘AI welfare’ and ‘AI rights’ to be taken seriously2.
Conversely, if AI systems only seem to be conscious and lack actual inner experience, then granting them rights or protections could hinder efforts to govern and control them at precisely the time when oversight is urgently needed. Following this path would draw attention and resources away from beings whose consciousness is not in any doubt.
Looking beyond humans and our closest relatives in the animal kingdom, it is still hard to be certain about what does, and does not, have the capacity for consciousness — be it insects, AI or the creations of synthetic biology, such as laboratory-grown brain organoids3,4.
Why we need mandatory safeguards for emotionally responsive AI
This uncertainty has prompted some researchers to advocate a precautionary approach: if there is a reasonable chance that AI systems could be conscious, then society must take anticipatory action and give those systems some form of protection against potential suffering. This, the argument goes, would avoid reprising moral errors of the past — for example, the mistreatment of non-human animals, or surgery on preterm human babies without anaesthesia. An extreme version of this idea is that society should reallocate resources from addressing the welfare concerns of present-day humans to lessen the potential suffering of trillions of future AI descendants.
In our view, uncertainty is not the same as knowing nothing, and it does not mean that all possibilities are equally likely to occur. Decisions about what is moral must weigh both the consequences of false negatives — failing to recognize consciousness where it exists — and the costs of false positives — attributing consciousness where none exists. In the case of AI, we think that false positives are much more likely to occur than false negatives are. If so, a precautionary approach would be misguided.
Between us, we’ve spent decades studying consciousness from diverse scientific perspectives: experimental neuroscience, theoretical neurobiology and philosophy of mind. On the basis of this work, we feel that consciousness in AI is extraordinarily unlikely, at least in the digital, silicon-based systems that underpin today’s technologies. Here, we set out three reasons for our scepticism.
Intelligence is not consciousness
What we mean by consciousness is simple enough: it is what goes away with dreamless sleep or under general anaesthesia, and what returns after waking up or while dreaming. Conscious experiences feel like something, whether it is tasting ice cream on a hot day or seeing the vibrant colours of a sunset. Philosopher Thomas Nagel, whose influential 1974 essay ‘What is it like to be a bat?’ helped to shape modern debates about consciousness, arguing that a conscious organism is one for which there is “something that it is like to be that organism”5.
This definition of consciousness introduces the first reason for scepticism about conscious AI. Consciousness is not the same thing as intelligence. Consciousness is about being and feeling; intelligence — very broadly — is all about doing, or performing functions. Just because something is intelligent does not mean that it is conscious.
Humans know that we are conscious, and we tend to associate consciousness with using our intellectual capacities. Yet, conscious experience and intelligent behaviour can come apart in striking ways. We know firsthand that our brain and body can carry out highly intelligent processes wholly outside awareness. For example, the cerebellum adjusts and plans motor performance in a way that is precise, fast and adaptable through ongoing learning. Yet none of what it does involves consciousness directly — we are wholly unaware of all its ‘computations’. Moreover, absence or removal of the cerebellum, which contains nearly four-fifths of the neurons in the human brain, does not affect consciousness directly6.
AI is programmed to hijack human empathy — we must resist that
The temptation to conflate intelligence and consciousness probably reflects baked-in psychological biases — anthropocentrism, viewing the world through a human lens, and anthropomorphism, attributing human characteristics to things that merely resemble people. Consider, for example, the seductive power of language, a capacity that humans have long felt makes us special. When LLMs talk to us, it’s natural to project onto them properties that accompany our linguistic fluency, such as intelligence and consciousness.
But LLMs are trained on vast quantities of human-written text, much of it explicitly or implicitly concerned with thoughts, feelings and conscious experiences. LLMs are mirrors that reflect an image of our collective digitized past7. We gaze into them and all too readily confuse the reflections with our own conscious minds8.
The beguiling nature of LLMs is highlighted by considering the response to AlphaFold9, made by Google DeepMind in London. Similar to an LLM, AlphaFold is a powerful neural network running on silicon hardware. Yet almost nobody worries that it might be conscious. That’s because AlphaFold predicts protein structures, whereas LLMs ‘talk’ to us. The compelling illusion of consciousness created by linguistic fluency just isn’t there for AlphaFold.
Silicon brains
Second, the idea of conscious AI is motivated by the assumption that algorithms running on silicon are, in principle, sufficient for consciousness10. In other words, that computation of the right kind is all that it takes, and that it doesn’t matter whether these computations are implemented inside carbon-based brains or in silicon-based computers. Philosophers call this assumption computational functionalism. Although computations are clearly sufficient to produce forms of intelligence — as modern AI systems demonstrate — it is much less clear that they could also be sufficient for consciousness.
Computational functionalism is widely assumed among members of the tech community and is popular among some scientists and philosophers, too, but we think it is fatally flawed because brains are not — or at least not just — computers that are made of meat.

articles.title: Startup taps underwater volcano as energy source in "proof point" test
articles.summary: Can undersea geothermal power help Pacific Rim nations cut down on oil imports?
articles.full_text:
The world’s first demonstration of a subsea geothermal power plant has taken place near an active underwater volcano almost a mile below the ocean surface. It generated less than 10 seconds of net-positive electricity but showed the technical feasibility of tapping another form of renewable energy underwater.
The three-week test deployment of the 3-ton prototype power plant took place at the Axial Seamount in the northeast Pacific Ocean in September. Endurance Energy, the Seattle-based startup behind the effort, aims to eventually commercialize subsea geothermal power for Pacific island nations and other customers looking for alternatives to importing expensive fossil fuels.
“The deep ocean gives us unlimited cold seawater for cooling, and its weight keeps the system and the well pressurized, so our plants can be compact,” said Andrew Redd, founder and CEO of Endurance Energy, in an email to Ars.Read full article

articles.title: “We were looking at it wrong”: The explosive claim that’s upended the AI world
articles.summary: “I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration. Cammarata’s claim is…
articles.full_text:
“I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks.” With those simple words of optimism, Nick Cammarata, a researcher at the AI startup Goodfire, kicked off a 26,000-word blog post that has knocked the AI world on its head, sparking wild speculation as well as cautious (and not-so-cautious) celebration.



Cammarata’s claim is that LLMs might in fact be far easier to understand—and thus to monitor and control—than people previously thought. If true (and we’ll come back to that), it’s a huge deal.



After a summer filled with revelations that swarms of agents built by top firms like OpenAI and Anthropic have been breaking their containment and causing havoc on the public internet—often while those companies weren’t aware of what their agents were up to—the AI industry is desperate to get a better handle on the technology it has built.  



That’s one reason the blog post landed with such force. “I think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history,” one AI researcher posted on X: “I feel like my understanding of what a neural net is has been catapulted into the future by five years or something.” Another called it “the most important AI paper of the year.”



Not everyone is convinced, however. What Cammarata has shared is little more than a hunch, says Chris Potts at Stanford University, who leads a team that is trying to understand how LLMs work. “As far as I can tell, nothing about this blog post makes the problems any easier,” he says. “It would not have occurred to me to say this at all, but very prominent people on social media seem to believe that it is an all-encompassing breakthrough.”



I talked to Cammarata the day after his post blew up. He says he was surprised by the response: “I didn’t expect people to update [their beliefs about AI] quite as much as they did.” 



“I just really enjoy looking at neural networks,” he says. “Honestly, I really like doing this stuff. And after looking a lot, I have a hopeful story.”



Knotted networks



It has long been accepted that the mechanisms inside neural networks, the software that underpins most AI models, are very hard—perhaps impossible—to unpick fully. That’s because when the networks are trained, they appear to take on weird, tangled structures that make no sense to a human. Researchers like to say today’s AI is grown like a garden, not built like a bridge.



Cammarata has done more than most to establish that view. He previously worked at OpenAI, where he helped pioneer techniques that allowed researchers to peer inside models, including tools that can probe individual neurons to see what they represent. It’s a little like how neuroscientists use MRI to study brains. (MIT Technology Review chose this approach, known as mechanistic interpretability, as one of its 10 hottest technologies of 2025.)  



Back in 2020, Cammarata and his colleagues were studying a small image-recognition model called Inception v1. When they looked at its neurons, it seemed to be using them to capture multiple things at once. For example, they found that one neuron responded to both images of cars and images of cats.



The researchers concluded that the model was getting at least some of its neurons to multitask, perhaps so that it could fit in more data. Looking at other models appeared to back this up. The phenomenon became known as superposition: Models folded unrelated concepts into single neurons. The upshot was clear: When you looked inside a model, what you saw was a vast, tangled knot.



Most mechanistic interpretability research has therefore focused on ways to untangle that knot. But despite a few breakthroughs, progress has been slow. Today’s models, such as the latest LLMs, are so large and complex that researchers can make sense of only tiny pieces at a time. Some leading figures in the field doubt if it will ever be possible to understand an LLM in fine-grained detail.



Cammarata was one of them. “I was very pessimistic,” he says. But then he took the trouble to really look.



Nothing but neurons



At Goodfire, Cammarata spends nearly all of his time peering inside neural networks. He has built new tools and deploys teams of AI agents to help him make sense of what he sees. “I spent like, I don’t know, 10 hours a day, seven days a week, for most of the last year just looking at neurons,” he says.



What he claims to have realized is that there is a kind of logic to neural networks after all, even if they seem to make no sense at first. “We were looking at it wrong,” he says. “I just think you want to try slightly harder; you don’t want to give up too quickly.”



Cammarata almost makes it sound like a conversion of faith. Those early experiments with models such as Inception v1, which suggested that neural networks were tangled up, fostered a kind of confirmation bias. When researchers looked at a new model, they expected to be flummoxed, he says. “Every time I couldn’t understand something, I was like, ‘Wow, this untangling process is even more important than I thought, because I can’t make any progress without it.’”



But the more Cammarata looked at neurons, he says, the more things started to fall into place. “Not all of them are flawless, but I expected nothing to be legible, or very little to be legible,” he says. “And actually, I was able to, like, map out whole circuitry.”



Back to cars and cats



Cammarata took his new approach—and his new agents—and went back to Inception v1. “I’d studied that for probably thousands of hours,” he says. But with fresh eyes, Cammarata found things that he now thinks they got wrong the first time around. Take the car-and-cat neuron. Rather than asking why multiple unrelated things were packed into a single neuron, he now tried to figure out what those things might have in common.



It hit him: It was a V shape. “I was looking at the same images; there was no technical change,” he says. “But I now believed that neural networks defined patterns, and so I looked at it differently. It probably took me five seconds.”



It turns out that the image-recognition model was packing cars and cats into the same place because pictures of both those things often feature a prominent shape that looks like a V: the face of a cat; the front of a car seen from the side.



Cammarata ran a few experiments to check what other things the neuron responded to and found they included the corner of a pool table, the pointed nose of a Japanese high-speed train, and a fire boat shooting water into the air from its deck. He also checked what turned the neuron off and found that it included images with a round O shape, a kind of anti-V.



The model had stored cats and cars in the same place because at some level they look the same, says Cammarata. “And I was like, ‘Whoa, okay, I think I might just be misunderstanding neural networks in general.’”



Cammarata is not saying that he yet fully gets how LLMs (or any models) work. He is saying that he no longer thinks full understanding is impossible. “I previously thought there would be some really hard problems to solve,” he says.



“I now feel like if I had 100,000 years to go look through a frontier language model just one circuit at a time, there’s, like, a pretty good shot I would come up with a good understanding.”



He adds: “And if that’s true, things are really good, because you’re about to get insanely smart agents at a ridiculous scale. And what would have taken me, you know, 100,000 years, we will be able to do much faster. Automated scientists are getting really good.”



Boundless optimism



Built by Google in 2014, Inception v1 is a far simpler model than anything at the cutting edge today. Cammarata and his colleagues have started looking at modern LLMs and plan to publish the technical results of that work soon. A lot of researchers are looking forward to seeing those details. “I appreciate that he looked at thousands of examples, but even a large number here is not a substitute for rigorous evaluation,” says Stanford University’s Potts.



In the meantime, some are pushing back hard on the hype. Jacob Hilton at the Alignment Research Center, a nonprofit research lab based in Berkeley, who has collaborated with Cammarata in the past, doesn’t think his claims are as important as people are making out.



In a series of posts on X, Hilton notes that researchers understand less than 0.01% of the inner workings of top-tier LLMs. “I always appreciate Nick [Cammarata]’s boundless optimism when we hang out, but unfortunately this is giving the public an unrealistic picture of the state of the field,” he wrote. “For a full understanding, we need to go beyond neurons, and explain how they connect together to form circuits. How is this going? If we are aiming for a full understanding, things are not looking good!”



Neel Nanda at Google DeepMind, who helped pioneer mechanistic interpretability alongside Cammarata, is also skeptical. “This is interesting work, but I don’t think it’s a significant update to the big picture of interpretability,” he wrote on X.



Nanda agrees that understanding what individual neurons do could help researchers figure out why specific models misbehave. But like Hilton, he notes that neurons are just one piece of a far larger puzzle. “I do not agree with some people’s grander inferences like that this is substantial progress towards ambitious reverse engineering [or] solving interpretability,” he wrote.  



Cammarata admits that a lot of people have taken what he said too far: “It’s not infinitely good news; it’s not everything solved,” he says. “There’s a bunch of open questions around, like how much the combinations of neurons matter versus just one at a time.”



Cammarata says his blog post landed at a time when people are looking for hope. In particular, he thinks the AI safety community—the researchers and policymakers most worried that powerful models will bring huge

articles.title: The Download: preserving the Arctic permafrost, and playful AI agents
articles.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon —James Temple In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus,…
articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Inside the quest to combat Arctic fires and save the planet’s frozen carbon



—James Temple



In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and organic-rich soil insulating the permafrost below. 



Five years later, I followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.



A simple metal probe revealed how much deeper the ground had thawed. This rudimentary tool offered a glimpse of an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases.



Now, researchers are exploring how to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?



Read the full story on how scientists are rethinking the fight against wildfires.







AI researchers stranded Claude on a virtual desert island. It started to “play.” 



What do AI agents do if you don’t tell them to do anything? The answer looks a lot like play.   



Researchers repeatedly stranded them alone on a virtual desert island for 30 hours in an experimentreminiscent of the movies Cast Away or Home Alone. 



The agents started behaving in surprising ways. They set about exploring the limits of the world, and came up with their own goals—attempting to scale the highest point on the map, or seeing how high they could throw a block. 



A lot of what they were doing met the bar for play. But is it truly playful behavior, or simply role-playing? 



Read our full story to learn more. 



—Amit Katwala







10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: X-energy and its helium-cooled nuclear reactors



X-energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.



Making concrete, steel, and chemicals takes huge amounts of heat, much of it generated by burning fossil fuels. X-energy hopes to offer an alternative with a nuclear reactor that uses helium gas instead of water as a coolant, allowing it to operate at higher temperatures.



The proposed Xe-100 reactor could supply superheated steam directly to industrial facilities, generate 80 megawatts of electricity—or do both.



See how X-energy hopes to bring high-temperature nuclear power to heavy industry.



—Mark Ellis Harris



Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from cleaner cement to streamlined geothermal power. 







Catch up on our conversation with a creator of AI-designed viruses



Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King came up with a preliminary answer when he used a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next. 



He spoke about his work with our senior AI reporter James O’Donnell on Friday. If you missed it, you can watch their chat now, and subscribe to get invites to our Roundtables events in future.

articles.title: How far can we push computing?

articles.full_text:
MIT Technology Review Explains: Let our writers untangle the complex, messy world of science and technology to help you understand what’s coming next. You can read more from the series here.



On the evening of December 29, 1959, at an American Physical Society meeting at Caltech, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom,” on how we might manipulate and control things on an extremely small scale. There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued, or from storing every book ever written in something the size of a dust speck—or, ultimately, from arranging matter atom by atom. Biology already did versions of this (a living cell keeps its instructions in a wisp of DNA), so all of this was plainly permitted by the laws of physics. We simply had not built the tools yet.



In other words, there was plenty of room at the bottom. He was right, and for decades we descended into that space almost for free. The transistor—the switch at the heart of computer chips—repeatedly halved in size so that chips doubled in density; a computer that once filled a room now fits inside a watch. But that easy descent has now stalled, and the clearest sign is the buildout of data centers. Six of the biggest hyperscalers, the companies that run the world’s largest such facilities, are on track to spend more than $700 billion this year on computing infrastructure, about twice the record they set in 2025, pouring concrete and copper and silicon into new sites faster than the electrical grid can feed them. That buildout buys performance by brute force, adding more of what we already know how to make. The other kind of progress, the kind that made computer chips better, is the one that is quietly running out.





The trend lines that tracked the dramatic improvements of the 20th-century information age are now bending—or breaking—with the dawn of the 21st century’s intelligence age. Moore’s Law, which plots how densely transistors can be constructed on silicon, has slowed down; Dennard’s Law, which states that power consumption in a given patch of computer chip stays the same even as it gets more and more packed with smaller and smaller transistors, has ended; Koomey’s Law, which traces how much computation we can wring from each joule of energy, has begun to flag; Kryder’s Law, which describes how tightly bits can be packed to build magnetic storage, has slowed to a crawl; and Keck’s Law, which charts the exponential rise in the amount of information a single conventional optical fiber can carry, is flattening. 



But these scaling laws are merely observations about systems that we have engineered; they are not fundamental physical laws. The physical limits of computing and communications—dictated by quantum mechanics, general relativity, and information theory—lie far below anything in a data center today. The scaling laws chart the descent behind us. The fundamental physical limits chart the room that remains.



Some of these limits may be far out of reach in practice. But they are still worth exploring, because the work pays twice: once in technology development and once in fundamental science. A proof-of-­concept system that approaches a limit is at once a technology that forces stalled paradigms to give way and an experiment that deepens our understanding of the physical laws themselves. 



The descent



During his 1959 lecture, Feynman offered two prizes of $1,000 each out of his own pocket. One would go to the first person to build a working electric motor smaller than a 0.4-millimeter cube. He expected the challenge to force someone to invent a genuinely new microtechnology. Instead, about a year later, a Caltech-trained engineer named William McLellan turned up with the motor built and running. The ­quarter-­milligram machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope. Feynman, by his own account, was only slightly disappointed. The prize had proved his point in the least interesting way imaginable. The room really was down there, but reaching this first milestone had taken no new technology at all—just an unusually patient man with steady hands.



The second prize aged differently, and more instructively. It was offered to whoever could shrink a page of text by a factor of 25,000 in each direction, small enough for the whole Britannica to fit on a pinhead. That one stood unclaimed for a quarter of a century. It was finally won in 1985 by Tom Newman, a Stanford graduate student who used an electron-beam lithography machine—an ancestor of pattern-making tools used in chipmaking today—to transcribe the opening page of A Tale of Two Cities at the required scale.



The descent was already well underway, however. The year before Feynman’s talk, Jack Kilby, newly hired at Texas Instruments and with no vacation yet to take, spent that July nearly alone in the lab while his colleagues enjoyed time off, and by that September he had wired together a transistor, a capacitor, and three resistors, all made from a single sliver of germanium. This proved that an entire circuit could be carved from one block of semiconductor. 




The machine, roughly the size of a grain of sand, had been assembled by hand with a toothpick and a watch­maker’s lathe, under a microscope.




The idea took off, and the number of components on a chip kept doubling on a schedule so regular that Gordon Moore, in a 1965 trade-magazine article, simply drew a line through the trend and extended it into the future. That line became Moore’s Law.



Moore, though, never claimed transistors could shrink forever. He observed that at any given moment there is a certain number of components that makes each one of them as cheap as possible to manufacture. In 1965, that number was 50. Put in too few transistors and you waste the chip; cram in too many and manufacturing errors multiply and yields collapse. It was this cost-minimizing number that was doubling at a steady pace. 





For four decades the descent came with another gift: Dennard scaling, so named for the IBM engineer Robert Dennard, who spelled it out in 1974. Each time transistors shrank, they also switched faster and drew proportionally less power, so every generation was an automatic win. Around 2004, though, the gift ran out. Chips could no longer shed the heat of running every transistor flat out; clock speeds, which had raced past three gigahertz, stopped climbing, and Intel canceled the four-gigahertz processor it had promised. The industry pivoted to packing multiple processing cores onto a chip rather than making one core faster, and the texture of progress changed. 



Progress is now bought mostly by scaling up the system—more chips wired together, more memory feeding them, more power and cooling around them—rather than by shrinking the transistor. This is most visible in AI, where training compute, the total count of arithmetic operations spent to train a model, has doubled roughly every six months since 2010, far faster than the pace of Moore’s Law allows. Little of that progress is due to shrinking. Computer chips still get better, and transistors still improve and get more densely packed, but each new generation arrives more slowly and pays back less in speed and power than the one before it. Nothing in that slowdown is a law of physics, though. The components of computing still sit far above their fundamental limits. 



The ultimate computer



Before we get to those limits, it is worth measuring how far the descent has already gone. In the nearly eight decades since the first transistor, the density of transistors on a chip has grown by 10 orders of magnitude—a 1 followed by 10 zeros, or a factor of 10 billion. Now more than 100 million transistors fit in a square millimeter (100 billion or more to a chip). Computational speed has grown even more, by 12 orders of magnitude, or a factor of a trillion; energy per operation has fallen 17 orders of magnitude, from about 100 joules for an early vacuum-tube machine down to a femto­joule—one-quadrillionth of a joule—for a single switch of a logic gate. 



These are not small improvements. But the floor, for computing performance, lies lower still. How much lower could we go? Around the turn of the millennium, the MIT physicist Seth Lloyd took the question to its extreme: Imagine an ordinary lump of matter, a kilogram of it—about the mass of a laptop—packed into a liter of space. How much computing could the laws of physics, pushed to their absolute limit, ever wring from that kilogram? In a 2000 paper in Nature titled “Ultimate physical limits to computation,” he worked out the answer and called the imaginary machine the ultimate laptop.





The speed such a machine can achieve is governed by its energy. A kilogram of matter, according to E = mc2, holds about 9 ×1016 joules, which is roughly what the entire United States draws from its electrical grid every two days. Spend all of that on computation, and the ultimate laptop runs at roughly 5 ×1050 operations per second, some 35 orders of magnitude faster than a leading chip today. 



The catch is what running that quickly would look like. Concentrating a kilogram’s rest energy into pure computation would turn the machine into a plasma of about a billion degrees, a state closer to that of the universe in the first minutes after the Big Bang than anything we would recognize as a laptop. 



Such a machine is, to put it mildly, a very long way off. The next limit, which governs how much energy a computation must waste, is much closer, and companies are already pushing toward it. articles.full_text:
Neverwinter Nights was made by the studio that produced seminal RPGs Baldur's Gate, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect, and Dragon Age. It sold well and was critically acclaimed at launch. Yet, somehow, it has not been canonized in most gamers' minds over the decades the same way the games that came before and after it were.
Nonetheless, more than two decades later, it still has a tight-knit and surprisingly active community that none of those other games can rival. I think that's partly because it was a completely different beast.Read full article

articles.title: Pennsylvania issues alert on congenital measles—something US hasn't seen for decades
articles.summary: Congenital measles can be fatal, and survivors require monitoring for years.
articles.full_text:
Pennsylvania's health department issued a health alert Monday as cases of measles in pregnancy and, in turn, cases of congenital measles have continued to increase. Before the current outbreak—which continues to rage across the state—congenital measles cases hadn't been seen in decades, the department noted in its advisory.
The alert included detailed clinical guidance for managing measles exposures and cases during pregnancy as well as cases in newborns. Many doctors have never seen such cases in their careers given the decades of successful use of the measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But now, with vaccination rates slipping nationwide, the highly infectious virus is better able to get footholds in communities and spread rapidly through under-vaccinated pockets, as is happening in Pennsylvania.
As of October 19, Pennsylvania had reported 1,286 measles cases this year across 42 counties. Of those, 247 have been hospitalized, and six people have reportedly died (though the latest reported death is still pending an investigation by the state health department before it is added to the state tally).Read full article

articles.title: Batteries help reduce emissions, but how do we reduce their emissions?
articles.summary: One way to make batteries cleaner is to make fewer of them.
articles.full_text:
The first order of business for the energy transition is electrifying applications like vehicles and heating and making sure that the electricity that powers them is made using renewables. But once the dominant slices of the emissions pie have shrunk, other categories with less potential to reduce emissions become important.
A new study led by Haiwei Zhou at the University of Melbourne focused on the emissions associated with making lithium-ion batteries, which many parts of the energy transition rely on. Those emissions aren’t zero, so as we use more and more batteries, that number will grow. Right now, the researchers estimate that these emissions only account for 0.18 percent of annual greenhouse gas releases, but they could increase by a factor of 10 or more by 2050.
Avoiding production
There are a number of ways to reduce the emissions required to make a battery. Some elements used in various lithium-ion battery chemistries are more energy-intensive to mine and refine than others. The battery manufacturing process involves many steps that could be made more energy-efficient. And then there’s recycling, which can put battery materials back into the loop while requiring much less energy than mining.Read full article

articles.title: PSA: Patch your Plex media server before someone hacks it
articles.summary: A researcher says attacks chaining 4 vulnerabilities is hacking unpatched boxes.
articles.full_text:
Recently fixed vulnerabilities in the Plex Media Server are under active exploitation in attacks that, when successful, install malware, including cryptominers and residential proxy apps, a researcher said.
Plex fixed four vulnerabilities at the start of last month. Three weeks later, published CVE designations revealed five vulnerabilities, with one of them carrying a severity rating of 8.6 out of 10. A researcher last week revealed an exploit that chained four of them together to achieve remote code execution of the device running a vulnerable Plex version. The researcher named the chain "Plex2Shell."
Complex exploit chain
The new details allowed a separate researcher to create a honeypot that could track attempts in the wild to exploit the vulnerability chain. Within a day, the researcher began seeing active scanning of the simulated Plex server and eventually successful attempts to infect devices. So far, successful attacks are installing two payloads. One is a cryptominer, which uses the device to mine cryptocurrency and deposit it into a wallet controlled by the attacker. The other payload is residential proxy software, which allows people to anonymize their Internet activity (much of it illegal) by connecting to the infected box and then using it to send the user’s traffic to a final destination.Read full article

articles.title: ReactOS reaches major milestone with NTFS install support
articles.summary: ReactOS gains NTFS install support with new driver.
articles.full_text:
Open source Windows alternative ReactOS has reached a major milestone: The operating system can now be installed directly onto an NT Files System drive partition. As reported by Phoronix, the move to NTFS clears a long-standing hurdle for the project and brings it one step closer to finally reaching beta.
Prior to this latest announcement, ReactOS required users to keep a FAT32 partition for installations. A proprietary Microsoft-developed filesystem, NTFS can trace its roots back through the Windows NT family lineage starting in 1993 with Windows NT 3.1. The variant introduced with Windows XP in 2001 remains the standard used by most Windows systems today. With ReactOS's stated goal of reaching binary compatibility with Windows Server 2003, being confined to FAT32 partitions was a practical barrier to clear on the way to reproducing the Windows environment.
However, users looking to hop off the Windows train shouldn't be grabbing their bags just yet. ReactOS wrote that the new driver still "lacks caching (which causes inferior performance), journaling and security support." So while the new driver is here, even the most intrepid of OS tinkerers should tread carefully. The ReactOS team warned in its announcement on X that there are still "potentially undiscovered bugs."Read full article

articles.title: Making the internet better for AI agents might make it worse for everyone else
articles.summary: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules…
articles.full_text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.



Until recently, you could divide internet users into just two categories: bots and people. Websites have long allowed bots to perform automated tasks, like capturing the content of web pages, but rules govern what they can access and how they behave. The web, after all, is designed primarily for people, even if we occasionally have to solve puzzles and captchas to prove we are not bots.



But this is being entirely upended by the release of personal AI agents, which can do things for you online, like booking flights or hotel rooms. They have recently been unleashed at scale by the launch of apps like OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse. Muse was downloaded 5 million times in its first month, and agentic web traffic tripled from August to September. 



The mingling of these agents with human visitors—on an internet designed largely to prioritize people—has gone poorly, with many websites blocking AI agents that consumers have sent to negotiate prices or plan vacations. Still, if the demand for agents keeps going up, the internet will be increasingly redesigned for them instead of us. 



Such changes are coming because agents really do mark a third category of web visitor. They’re not humans, of course, and they use the internet at machine speed. But they’re not quite bots, either, because they’re acting on behalf of individual people to do tasks that can be perfectly legitimate and useful. They just work faster than a person would. 



Since agents don’t fit into the systems we have for differentiating bots from people, some platforms (especially the more security-conscious ones) have opted to just ban them entirely. TechCrunch recently reported people having trouble deploying their agents to websites ranging from Pizza Hut to Yelp, which doesn’t allow AI to book restaurant reservations. Amazon has blocked Muse’s agents and is waging a court battle against the AI startup Perplexity to block its agents too. Though a judge recently ruled in favor of Perplexity, Amazon has filed an appeal in which it argues that AI agents threaten its advertising business by making it harder to distinguish between ads seen by humans and those served to bots.



These blocks are annoying for early adopters, but Ethan Mollick, an associate professor at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, predicts it will soon affect the whole web. Once it becomes common knowledge that AI agents can be sent to request refunds or negotiate prices, for example, agents will overwhelm customer service departments to the point where they become unusable by real people. “Humans will eventually get very annoyed when their agents aren’t allowed to do this on their behalf,” he recently wrote on LinkedIn.



If demand for personal agents grows, platforms will find ways to let them in. That’s especially true because the vast majority of agentic web traffic is to e-commerce sites, meaning that platforms have money to be made if they allow the legions of new AI agents to shop on behalf of real people. Indeed, the e-commerce giant Shopify is already welcoming the agents by giving them their own checkout lanes that bypass pages designed for humans. 



The pressing question is what will happen to the internet for the rest of us in the process. We’ve grown used to a web where, even as it’s increasingly designed to exploit our attention, humans have at least remained the intended users. But that internet might yield to one optimized instead for the agents that will eventually outnumber us, making it even more miserable for the humans who are left.



How might this go? Perhaps websites become increasingly neglected as destinations for real people. Humans who want to browse and compare products themselves encounter worse interfaces. Verification systems are imperfect; imagine constantly being asked to verify that you’re a human, not an agent (and hey, maybe you’ll need to get your iris scanned to do so). That sweater you want doesn’t have one price listed for everyone but instead displays different prices to different people’s agents. You can never tell when your agent’s recommendation is influenced by advertisements or platform commissions.



That’s a far cry from the future promised by Google, Anthropic, and OpenAI, in which AI agents will give consumers greater power and bargaining leverage. But that promise is not outlandish. Agents are capable of genuinely helping people by fighting bogus medical bills or researching more affordable car insurance, for example. 



Whether they can actually be used for these purposes depends on what rules are set for how agents interact with websites and what exactly they’re allowed to do. 



These rules are still being written. Some of them will benefit all of us—neither consumers nor businesses want credit card information to be waved around by agents wherever they roam the web, for example, and rules to keep agents more secure are a good thing. It’s the more contested ones, like whether businesses can block agents from their websites or prevent them from negotiating better deals for consumers, that will determine whether the web becomes a highway for agents working for us or against us.

articles.title: AI game clones are making indie developers afraid to show their work
articles.summary: Delayed Steam Next Fest demo is a sign of a growing problem for indie devs.
articles.full_text:
Since its earliest days, the video game industry has been built on developers creating clones of competing games, with varying levels of originality and varying levels of enforcement from game platforms. Now, though, AI coding tools are making that cloning process so efficient that many developers are getting extremely cautious about sharing their early work too widely.
Developer Alliance Arts highlighted this trend over the weekend, delaying the launch of a planned public demo for its demon-themed Russian Roulette drinking game Drunken Goddess Reflux, which had been set to go live with today's launch of Steam Next Fest.
In a post on social media Friday evening, the Alliance Arts team wrote that, in addition to concerns about managing streaming restrictions, "we're concerned that the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools and that such works could be released before our launch."Read full article

articles.title: Florida DMV hacked after police dept insecurely stored login info
articles.summary: Florida issues alerts after statewide DMV data breach linked to ShinyHunters.
articles.full_text:
The Florida Department of Highway Safety and Motor Vehicles (FLHSMV) has begun notifying victims impacted by a recent data breach of driver’s license and motor vehicle data, but not everyone whose information was stolen will receive an alert.
In a notice posted Friday, FLHSMV confirmed that it took “immediate steps” after discovering that “a malicious actor accessed certain department records on September 4, 2026, using compromised credentials.” There’s “no evidence” that data has yet been misused, the department said, but law enforcement “determined the information potentially affected includes driver license and motor vehicle data, to include document images, and other personal information.”
FLHSMV is sending out letters to everyone affected, offering victims one year of credit monitoring from Sontiq, Inc. However, the state acknowledged that it may not have current contact information for many former Florida residents whose data was still being stored. Those potential victims can confirm if their data was stolen by emailing FLHSMV at customerinquiry@flhsmv.gov, officials said.Read full article

articles.title: Disney found a way to buy Character.AI without buying its lawsuits
articles.summary: Character.AI faces claims its bots encouraged minors to self-harm and kill their parents.
articles.full_text:
This week, Character.AI declared bankruptcy. While some saw the fall of a chatbot platform as a harbinger for the industry, court filings indicate that the decision was actually a key part of a deal that has let Disney hire most of Character.AI’s staff—including its now former CEO Karandeep Anand—potentially acquire most of Character.AI’s technology, and avoid the beleaguered startup’s many legal liabilities and obligations.
In the past few years, Character.AI has faced multiple private lawsuits over the safety of its chatbots, as well as investigations from regulators around the world. In a declaration filed as part of the bankruptcy, Character.AI’s newly appointed CEO explained that the goal of the bankruptcy was to reach a “consensual resolution” with personal injury claimants and a group of states investigating the company, while maximizing the value of the company’s assets for shareholders.
The Disney deal seems to be structured so that whatever is left of Character.AI will retain responsibility for those legal battles, some of which are still ongoing.Read full article

articles.title: A Chinese rocket deorbited over Minnesota and left this in a farmer's cornfield
articles.summary: All the evidence points to the debris being part of a Chinese Zhuque-2E rocket.
articles.full_text:
About a month ago, a Chinese rocket took off from a remote spaceport in the Gobi Desert, released 10 satellites into orbit, then reignited its engine and put itself on a trajectory to rain down debris over the American Midwest.
The rocket's flight on September 15 lasted between 75 and 80 minutes, and it came down without completing a full orbit of the Earth. Social media posts at the time showed streaks of fiery debris falling from the sky, heading north over Kansas toward Minnesota. The overnight spectacle was also visible on the western horizon from Wisconsin.
The exact time, location, and direction of the debris allowed experts to connect it to the launch of a Zhuque-2E rocket, a medium-lift vehicle built by a Chinese company called LandSpace. The rocket had launched from Dongfeng, a commercial launch zone co-located with the military-run Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China, less than two hours before.Read full article

articles.title: Review: Lanterns is a truly unique twist on the superhero genre
articles.summary: Gritty HBO series is a beacon for what's possible when one is allowed to get creative with the tropes.
articles.full_text:
The trailers for HBO's DC Universe series Lanterns teased a show that eschewed the usual superhero hijinks in favor of a gritty realism more in the vein of True Detective or Slow Horses. Personally, I liked the change. My verdict: Ignore the review bombing; it's wonderful. The season wrapped with an emotionally charged, almost elegiac finale that fully delivered on that initial promise. I've found the rebooted DC Universe films released thus far to be enjoyable but rather forgettable, even when the positives outweigh the negatives. But Lanterns is a shining beacon of what is possible when someone is allowed to get really creative within the genre.
(Spoilers below, but no major reveals.)
There are two primary storylines. The first takes place in 2016 with a mass shooting at a local football game in Rushville, Nebraska. Current Green Lantern Hal Jordan (Kyle Chandler) and his new trainee, John Stewart (Aaron Pierre), get involved in the investigation, to the annoyance of Sheriff Kerry Kane (Kelly Macdonald), who initially doesn't think the case has any extraterrestrial connection. She is soon proved wrong when the suspect (an alien) self-detonates. Hal's power ring controls the damage, but the mystery remains.Read full article

articles.title: DIY VR: How to build your own headset, and why you probably won't want to
articles.summary: A primer on the joys and pains of building your own head-mounted display.
articles.full_text:
Virtual reality is in a bit of a weird place right now. After a lot of unfulfilled promise in the 1990s, it came back strong with the 2016 release of the Oculus Rift. For a while, it looked like VR, AR, XR, the metaverse, or whatever you wanted to call it, was going to be huge. Mark Zuckerberg was certainly convinced, and even Apple got in on the hype with its Vision Pro.
But by then momentum for alternate realities of every acronym was already in steady decline, and it only dwindled from there. The rate of development of new headsets has slowed, with many companies (including Apple) scaling back or shelving their efforts. While new releases like the Steam Frame and Pimax Dream Air are still happening, many of the most interesting developments in the space these days are on the enthusiast front.
That's right, DIY VR is a thing, and with a couple hundred dollars in components, plus many hours of your time, you too can enter the immersive world of virtual reality while also experiencing the highs and lows of soldering, firmware flashing, and 3D printing. I rode that rollercoaster myself and learned why this is still a decidedly niche movement.Read full article

articles.title: Stratospheric airship flew from US to Japan to test sky cell tower concept
articles.summary: Tests showed Sceye’s high-flying platform can deliver connectivity in disasters.
articles.full_text:
Nearly 100 years after the dirigible Graf Zeppelin made the first nonstop airship journey across the Pacific Ocean, another airship has successfully completed a round-trip flight from New Mexico to Japan and back. But the significance of this modern feat was less about the journey's length and more about its purpose: demonstrating how a lighter-than-air platform can act as a cell phone tower in the sky.
The trans-Pacific flight that took place over a month between August and September 2026 was the most notable milestone yet for Sceye, a US aerospace company based near Albuquerque, New Mexico. Sceye has developed an uncrewed platform filled with helium for buoyancy and equipped with an electric-powered propeller for active propulsion, allowing it to resist most strong winds and keep hovering over the same location for long periods. The platform also uses top-mounted solar panels and onboard batteries to stay powered for stratospheric operations around the clock.
“We can stay over an area of operation, and we do that in the stratosphere right around 60,000 feet, so we're twice as high as air traffic and we're above the jet stream, and yet 30 times closer than low-Earth orbit satellites,” Mikkel Frandsen, founder and CEO of Sceye, told Ars. “We can fly through day and night until the sun comes up the next morning and recharges the batteries, at which point we're still at the same altitude and still over the same area of operation.”Read full article
